Given: Structures: CH₃CHClCH₂CH₃; CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃; CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂Cl; (CH₃)₂CHCl; (CH₃)₂CHOH; CH₃CHClCHClCH₃; open-chain glucose with C2–C5 asymmetric.
Step 1: In 2-chlorobutane, C2 carries H, Cl, CH₃ and C₂H₅ — four different groups.
Step 2: In 2-chloropropane, C2 carries two CH₃ groups ⇒ not asymmetric.
Step 3: 2,3-Dichlorobutane has two asymmetric carbons (C2, C3); open-chain glucose has four (C2–C5).
Why: Chirality requires an atom (or arrangement) with no internal mirror symmetry; two identical groups on a carbon provide such symmetry.
Why not the others: (A) Those molecules have no asymmetric carbon. (B) A racemic mixture has zero rotation. (D) Enantiomers share all scalar physical properties.
Key point: Four different groups on a carbon ⇒ chiral; racemic mixture ⇒ zero rotation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Products and masses from cleaving methoxyethane with HI, and choosing the right Williamson route for an unsymmetrical ether with a tertiary group
questions.question: 6.0 g of methoxyethane (CH₃OC₂H₅, M = 60) is treated with one equivalent of HI in the cold. Which statement about the products and about preparing ethers is correct (I = 127)?
options: A) Products are ethyl iodide and methanol: 15.6 g C₂H₅I; tert-butyl methyl ether is best made from (CH₃)₃CBr and CH₃ONa
B) Products are CH₃I and C₂H₅I only; no alcohol forms
C) Products are methanol and ethanol, because HI hydrolyses ethers

D) Products are CH₃I (14.2 g, 0.10 mol) and ethanol (4.6 g), because I⁻ attacks the less hindered methyl carbon of the protonated ether by SN2; for tert-butyl methyl ether, the Williamson route must use sodium tert-butoxide with CH₃Br, since (CH₃)₃CBr with CH₃ONa gives mainly 2-methylpropene by elimination
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) CH₃I 14.2 g + ethanol 4.6 g; use (CH₃)₃CONa + CH₃Br.
Concept: Ethers are least reactive of the functional groups; the cleavage of the C–O bond in ethers takes place under drastic conditions with excess of hydrogen halides. In the reaction of an ether with HI, the ether is first protonated; iodide, a good nucleophile, then attacks the least substituted carbon of the oxonium ion by an SN2 mechanism, so with a mixed ether of primary groups the alkyl iodide formed is the one with the smaller alkyl group. In the Williamson synthesis, an alkyl halide is allowed to react with sodium alkoxide; better results are obtained if the alkyl halide is primary. In the case of secondary and tertiary alkyl halides, elimination competes over substitution; if a tertiary alkyl halide is used, an alkene is the only reaction product and no ether is formed.
Given: m = 6.0 g, M = 60 ⇒ 0.10 mol; M(CH₃I) = 142, M(C₂H₅OH) = 46.
Formula/Principle: CH₃OC₂H₅ + HI → CH₃I + C₂H₅OH.
Step 1: n(CH₃I) = n(C₂H₅OH) = 0.10 mol.
Step 2: m(CH₃I) = 0.10 × 142 = 14.2 g.
Step 3: m(C₂H₅OH) = 0.10 × 46 = 4.6 g.
Why: SN2 attack is fastest at the least hindered carbon; tertiary halides undergo elimination with strong bases such as alkoxides.
Why not the others: (A) Iodide attacks the methyl group, and that Williamson route gives an alkene. (B) One equivalent of HI gives one alkyl iodide and one alcohol. (C) HI cleaves ethers to an alkyl iodide and an alcohol.
Key point: R–O–CH₃ + HI → CH₃I + ROH (SN2 at methyl); Williamson: alkoxide of the bulky group + primary halide.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Mechanistic evidence and reactions of carboxylic acids: acyl–oxygen cleavage in esterification shown by ¹⁸O labelling, Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky α-halogenation, conversion to acid chlorides and reduction
questions.question: Which statement about carboxylic acids is correct?
options: A) When ethanoic acid is esterified with ethanol labelled with ¹⁸O, the ¹⁸O appears in the ester, not in the water, showing that the acid loses its –OH (acyl–oxygen bond breaks) while the alcohol keeps its oxygen; with Cl₂ and red phosphorus, ethanoic acid gives chloroethanoic acid by substitution of an α-hydrogen (HVZ reaction); SOCl₂ converts acids into acyl chlorides with SO₂ and HCl as gaseous by-products; LiAlH₄ reduces acids to primary alcohols
B) In esterification, the alcohol loses its –OH group, so the ¹⁸O ends up in the water
C) The HVZ reaction replaces the –OH of the carboxyl group by a halogen
D) LiAlH₄ reduces carboxylic acids to alkanes
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ¹⁸O stays in the ester (acyl–O cleavage); HVZ α-halogenation; SOCl₂ → acyl chloride; LiAlH₄ → 1° alcohol.
Concept: Carboxylic acids are esterified with alcohols or phenols in the presence of a mineral acid such as conc. H₂SO₄ or HCl gas as a catalyst. In the mechanism, protonation of the carbonyl oxygen activates the carbonyl group towards nucleophilic addition of the alcohol; proton transfer in the tetrahedral intermediate converts the –OH group into –OH₂⁺, which, being a better leaving group, is eliminated as a neutral water molecule; the protonated ester so formed finally loses a proton to give the ester. Carboxylic acids having an α-hydrogen are halogenated at the α-position on treatment with chlorine or bromine in the presence of a small amount of red phosphorus to give α-halocarboxylic acids (Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky reaction). Carboxylic acids react with PCl₅, PCl₃ and SOCl₂ to form acyl chlorides; thionyl chloride is preferred because the other two products are gaseous and escape the reaction mixture, making purification easy. Carboxylic acids are reduced to primary alcohols by lithium aluminium hydride or better with diborane.
Given: R–CO–OH + H–¹⁸O–R′ → R–CO–¹⁸O–R′ + H₂O.
Why: The alcohol is the nucleophile that adds to the carbonyl carbon, so its oxygen becomes the ester oxygen; the leaving water carries the acid's original –OH.
Why not the others: (B) The labelled oxygen stays in the ester. (C) HVZ substitutes an α-H, not the –OH. (D) The product is a primary alcohol.
Key point: Esterification: acid's –OH leaves; HVZ: α-halogenation; SOCl₂ → RCOCl; LiAlH₄ → RCH₂OH.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Reading pKb values of aromatic and aliphatic amines to rank their basicity and explaining the order by lone-pair delocalisation and substituent effects
questions.question: pKb values in water: methylamine 3.38, benzylamine 4.70, p-toluidine (p-methylaniline) 8.92, N-methylaniline 9.30, aniline 9.38, p-nitroaniline 13.0. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) Aniline is the strongest base because its lone pair is part of an aromatic ring
B) Benzylamine is weaker than aniline, because both contain a benzene ring
C) p-Nitroaniline is more basic than aniline, because –NO₂ donates electrons

D) Basicity order: methylamine > benzylamine > p-toluidine > N-methylaniline > aniline > p-nitroaniline (lower pKb = stronger base); in arylamines the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the ring, so they are much weaker than alkylamines; in benzylamine the –NH₂ is separated from the ring by a CH₂ group, so its lone pair is not delocalised; an electron-releasing –CH₃ at the para position slightly increases basicity, while electron-withdrawing –NO₂ strongly decreases it
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Methylamine > benzylamine > p-toluidine > N-methylaniline > aniline > p-nitroaniline.
Concept: The larger the value of Kb or the smaller the value of pKb, the stronger the base. Aniline is a weaker base than ammonia because in aniline the –NH₂ group is attached directly to the benzene ring, which results in the unshared electron pair on the nitrogen atom being in conjugation with the benzene ring and thus making it less available for protonation. In substituted anilines, electron-releasing groups like –OCH₃ and –CH₃ increase basic strength, whereas electron-withdrawing groups like –NO₂, –SO₃H, –COOH and –X decrease it. Alkylamines are stronger bases than ammonia due to the +I effect of the alkyl groups.
Given: pKb values as listed.
Step 1: Arrange by increasing pKb: 3.38 < 4.70 < 8.92 < 9.30 < 9.38 < 13.0.
Step 2: Benzylamine (pKb 4.70) is an alkylamine in character — the ring is not conjugated with nitrogen.
Step 3: The nitro group delocalises the lone pair further by its –R effect, lowering basicity by about 10⁴ times (pKb 13.0 vs 9.38).
Why: Basicity measures how available the nitrogen lone pair is for a proton; anything that delocalises or withdraws it lowers basicity.
Why not the others: (A) Delocalisation into the ring makes aniline weak. (B) Benzylamine's nitrogen is not conjugated with the ring, so it is the stronger base. (C) –NO₂ withdraws electrons.
Key point: Lower pKb = stronger base; arylamines ≪ alkylamines; –CH₃ raises, –NO₂ lowers aniline basicity.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Distinguishing glucose from fructose with bromine water, why both reduce Tollens' reagent, oxidation of glucose with nitric acid, and the meaning of D/L versus the sign of rotation
questions.question: Which statement about glucose and fructose is correct?
options: A) Bromine water oxidises glucose to gluconic acid (its –CHO becomes –COOH) but does not oxidise fructose, so it distinguishes an aldose from a ketose; both nevertheless reduce Tollens' and Fehling's reagents, because in alkaline solution fructose (an α-hydroxyketone) isomerises through an enediol; nitric acid oxidises glucose to saccharic acid (both terminal carbons become –COOH); both are D-sugars, yet glucose is dextrorotatory and fructose laevorotatory, since D/L refers to configuration relative to glyceraldehyde, not to the sign of rotation
B) Fructose is oxidised by bromine water to a ketonic acid; glucose is not affected
C) Fructose does not reduce Tollens' reagent, because it is a ketose
D) D-fructose must be dextrorotatory, because D means dextrorotatory
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Bromine water oxidises only glucose; both reduce Tollens' reagent; HNO₃ gives saccharic acid; D/L is configuration, not rotation.
Concept: Glucose gets oxidised to a six-carbon carboxylic acid (gluconic acid) on reaction with a mild oxidising agent like bromine water, indicating that the carbonyl group is present as an aldehydic group. On oxidation with nitric acid, glucose as well as gluconic acid both yield a dicarboxylic acid, saccharic acid, indicating the presence of a primary alcoholic (–OH) group in glucose. Fructose is a ketohexose. All monosaccharides, whether aldoses or ketoses, are reducing sugars. The letters 'D' or 'L' before the name of any compound indicate the relative configuration of a particular stereoisomer, referring to its relation with a particular isomer of glyceraldehyde; the –OH on the lowest asymmetric carbon on the right side corresponds to the D-series. It may be remembered that D- and L- have no relation with the optical activity of the compound; they are also not related to the letters 'd' and 'l'. Fructose is laevorotatory; glucose is dextrorotatory.
Given: Glucose: aldohexose; fructose: ketohexose.
Step 1: Bromine water is a mild, non-alkaline oxidant that attacks only –CHO.
Step 2: Tollens'/Fehling's reagents are alkaline; fructose enolises and forms aldehydic species, so it reduces them too.
Step 3: D-glucose is (+) and D-fructose is (−), both D.
Why: Bromine water works in neutral/acidic medium where fructose cannot rearrange, so it is the test that separates aldoses from ketoses.
Why not the others: (B) Reversed. (C) Fructose is a reducing sugar. (D) D/L is unrelated to the sign of rotation.
Key point: Bromine water: aldose test; all monosaccharides reduce Tollens'; D/L ≠ (+)/(−).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Identifying the limiting reagent when marble chips react with hydrochloric acid and calculating the CO₂ formed, the mass loss and the unreacted solid
questions.question: 10.0 g of CaCO₃ (M = 100) is added to 50.0 mL of 2.00 M HCl in a flask on a balance. CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂. Which result is correct (molar volume 22.4 L at STP)?
options: A) CaCO₃ is limiting; 0.10 mol CO₂ (4.4 g) forms; no solid remains
B) Neither reagent is limiting, since equal moles are present; 2.24 L CO₂ forms

C) HCl is limiting: 0.100 mol HCl reacts with 0.050 mol CaCO₃, giving 0.050 mol CO₂ (2.2 g, 1.12 L at STP), so the balance reading falls by 2.2 g; 5.0 g of CaCO₃ remains unreacted, and 5.55 g of CaCl₂ forms
D) HCl is limiting; 0.10 mol CO₂ forms; 0 g CaCO₃ remains
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) HCl limiting; 2.2 g (1.12 L) CO₂; 5.0 g CaCO₃ left; 5.55 g CaCl₂.
Concept: The reactant which is present in the lesser amount relative to the stoichiometric requirement gets consumed after some time and after that no further reaction takes place whatever the amount of the other reactant present; hence the reactant which gets consumed limits the amount of product formed and is called the limiting reagent. In an open flask, escaping CO₂ causes a loss of mass equal to the mass of CO₂ evolved.
Given: n(CaCO₃) = 10.0/100 = 0.100 mol; n(HCl) = 0.0500 × 2.00 = 0.100 mol; ratio needed 1 : 2.
Formula/Principle: Compare available moles with the stoichiometric ratio.
Step 1: 0.100 mol CaCO₃ would need 0.200 mol HCl; only 0.100 mol present ⇒ HCl limiting.
Step 2: CaCO₃ reacting = 0.050 mol; CO₂ = 0.050 mol = 2.2 g = 1.12 L at STP.
Step 3: CaCO₃ left = 0.050 mol = 5.0 g; CaCl₂ = 0.050 × 111 = 5.55 g.
Why: Equal moles do not mean equal stoichiometric amounts; HCl is needed twice over.
Why not the others: (A) CaCO₃ is in excess. (B) The 1 : 2 ratio makes HCl limiting. (D) Only half the CaCO₃ reacts, giving 0.050 mol CO₂.
Key point: Divide moles by stoichiometric coefficients; the smallest quotient is the limiting reagent.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Counting orbitals and electrons allowed by sets of quantum numbers, nodal planes of d orbitals, and filling order by the (n + l) rule
questions.question: Which statement about quantum numbers is correct?
options: A) The shell n = 4 has 4 orbitals and 8 electrons; 4p fills before 3d because it has the higher n

B) The shell n = 4 has 16 orbitals and holds 32 electrons; 4 electrons can have n = 3 and m_l = +1 (one orbital each from 3p and 3d); the 3d_xy orbital has two nodal planes (the xz and yz planes); by the (n + l) rule 4s (n + l = 4) fills before 3d (5), and 3d before 4p (both 5, lower n first); the subshells with n + l = 5 (3d, 4p, 5s) can hold 18 electrons in all
C) Electrons with n = 3 and m_l = +1 number 6, since every subshell of n = 3 has an m_l = +1 orbital
D) The d_xy orbital has no nodal planes; the (n + l) rule fills 3d before 4s
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 16 orbitals/32 electrons for n = 4; 4 electrons with n = 3, m_l = +1; d_xy has 2 nodal planes; 4s < 3d < 4p; 18 electrons for n + l = 5.
Concept: For a given n, l takes values 0 to n − 1, and for a given l, m_l takes values −l … 0 … +l, giving 2l + 1 orbitals; the total number of orbitals in a shell is n², and each orbital holds two electrons with opposite spins. The number of angular nodes is given by l; d orbitals (l = 2) have two nodal planes (for d_xy these are the xz and yz planes). The energy of an orbital in multi-electron atoms depends on n + l: the lower the value of (n + l), the lower the energy; if two orbitals have the same value of (n + l), the orbital with lower n has lower energy.
Given: Quantum number rules as stated.
Formula/Principle: Orbitals in shell n = n²; for each l there are 2l + 1 values of m_l; angular nodes = l; filling order by (n + l), then n.
Step 1: n = 4: n² = 16 orbitals ⇒ 32 electrons.
Step 2: n = 3, m_l = +1: l = 1 (3p) and l = 2 (3d) each have one such orbital (3s has only m_l = 0) ⇒ 2 orbitals ⇒ 4 electrons.
Step 3: n + l = 5: 3d (10) + 4p (6) + 5s (2) = 18 electrons.
Why: The quantum numbers are linked: each choice restricts the next, so counting must respect l < n and |m_l| ≤ l.
Why not the others: (A) Miscounts the shell, and 4p fills after 3d. (C) 3s has no m_l = +1 orbital. (D) d orbitals have two angular nodes, and 4s fills before 3d.
Key point: Orbitals per shell = n²; angular nodes = l; fill by increasing n + l, then increasing n.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity; s and p block trends
questions.sub_topic: Explaining the structures of elemental nitrogen and phosphorus, oxygen and sulphur, the low F–F bond enthalpy, and the absence of NCl₅ from atomic size and available orbitals
questions.question: Which explanation of p-block structures is correct?
options: A) Phosphorus exists as P₂ with a triple bond like N₂, because it is in the same group
B) Fluorine has the highest bond enthalpy among the halogens, because it is the smallest

C) Nitrogen forms N₂ with a strong triple bond because its small size allows effective pπ–pπ overlap, whereas phosphorus, being larger, forms P₄ tetrahedra with single bonds; similarly oxygen is diatomic O₂ while sulphur forms S₈ rings; the F–F bond is weaker than Cl–Cl because of strong repulsion between the lone pairs of the small F atoms; nitrogen cannot form NCl₅ because it has no d orbitals in its valence shell to expand its covalency beyond four, whereas phosphorus forms PCl₅
D) Nitrogen forms NCl₅ readily, because it is more electronegative than phosphorus
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Small first-row atoms form multiple pπ–pπ bonds; larger atoms form single-bonded networks; lone-pair repulsion weakens F–F; N lacks d orbitals.
Concept: Nitrogen differs from the rest of the members of its group due to its small size, high electronegativity, high ionisation enthalpy and non-availability of d orbitals. Nitrogen has the unique ability to form pπ–pπ multiple bonds with itself and with other elements having small size and high electronegativity; heavier elements of this group do not form pπ–pπ bonds as their atomic orbitals are so large and diffuse that they cannot have effective overlapping. Thus nitrogen exists as a diatomic molecule with a triple bond, while phosphorus exists as P₄. Oxygen exists as diatomic O₂ while sulphur exists as S₈. The bond dissociation enthalpy of F₂ is smaller than that of Cl₂, mainly due to the relatively large electron–electron repulsion among the lone pairs in the F₂ molecule, where they are much closer to each other than in Cl₂. Nitrogen cannot form pentahalides because the maximum covalency of nitrogen is four, as only four (one s and three p) orbitals are available for bonding; the heavier elements have vacant d orbitals in the outermost shell which can be used for bonding (covalency), e.g. PF₅, PCl₅.
Given: Bond enthalpies: F–F 158, Cl–Cl 242 kJ mol⁻¹.
Why: Atomic size controls both π overlap and lone-pair repulsion, and the valence shell of second-period atoms has only s and p orbitals.
Why not the others: (A) P₄ with single bonds is the stable form. (B) F–F is weaker than Cl–Cl. (D) Nitrogen's covalency is limited to four.
Key point: Second-period atoms: strong pπ–pπ bonds, no d orbitals; heavier atoms: single-bonded networks, expanded valence.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Relating bond enthalpy to bond order for N₂, O₂ and F₂, ordering bond angles by lone-pair repulsion, and the trend in H–X bond enthalpy and length
questions.question: Which statement about bond parameters is correct, with the right reason?
options: A) Bond enthalpy decreases N≡N (946 kJ mol⁻¹, bond order 3) > O=O (498, bond order 2) > F–F (158, bond order 1) because a higher bond order means a stronger, shorter bond; bond angles decrease CH₄ (109.5°) > NH₃ (107°) > H₂O (104.5°) because lone pairs repel bonding pairs more than bonding pairs repel one another; H–X bond enthalpy decreases HF > HCl > HBr > HI as the bond length increases with the size of X
B) Bond enthalpy increases with decreasing bond order; H₂O has the largest bond angle of the three hydrides
C) HI has the strongest H–X bond, because iodine is the largest
D) All three hydrides CH₄, NH₃ and H₂O have the same bond angle, because all are sp³ hybridised
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Bond enthalpy rises with bond order; lone pairs squeeze bond angles; H–X bonds weaken down the group.
Concept: Bond length is defined as the equilibrium distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms; bond enthalpy is the amount of energy required to break one mole of bonds of a particular type between two atoms in a gaseous state; bond order is the number of bonds between two atoms. With increase in bond order, bond enthalpy increases and bond length decreases. According to VSEPR theory, the repulsive interactions decrease in the order lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair; hence, although CH₄, NH₃ and H₂O all have tetrahedral electron-pair arrangements, the bond angle decreases from 109.5° to 107° to 104.5° as the number of lone pairs increases from 0 to 2.
Given: Bond enthalpies N₂ 946, O₂ 498, F₂ 158 kJ mol⁻¹; angles 109.5°, 107°, 104.5°.
Why: More shared pairs hold atoms closer and more strongly; lone pairs, held by only one nucleus, spread out more and push bonds together; larger halogen atoms give longer, weaker bonds with hydrogen.
Why not the others: (B) Reversed relationships. (C) HI has the weakest H–X bond. (D) Lone pairs change the angles.
Key point: Bond order ↑ ⇒ enthalpy ↑, length ↓; lone pairs reduce bond angles; H–X strength falls down the group.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Measuring the enthalpy of neutralisation in a constant-pressure calorimeter from a temperature rise, using mass, specific heat and moles of water formed
questions.question: 50.0 mL of 1.00 M HCl and 50.0 mL of 1.00 M NaOH, both at 25.0 °C, are mixed in an insulated cup; the temperature rises to 31.8 °C. Take the solution's mass as 100 g and specific heat 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹, and neglect the cup's heat capacity. Which result is correct?
options: A) q = 28.4 kJ; ΔH = −28.4 kJ mol⁻¹, measured at constant volume

B) q = 2.84 kJ for 0.0500 mol of water formed, so ΔH(neutralisation) = −56.8 kJ mol⁻¹; since the cup is open to the atmosphere, the heat measured is q_p = ΔH; for an ideal gas the molar heat capacities are related by Cp − Cv = R
C) q = 2.84 kJ for 0.100 mol of water, so ΔH = −28.4 kJ mol⁻¹
D) q = 1.42 kJ; ΔH = +56.8 kJ mol⁻¹, because the temperature rose
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) q = 2.84 kJ; ΔH = −56.8 kJ mol⁻¹ (constant pressure).
Concept: Heat absorbed or released can be measured from the temperature change: q = mcΔT, where c is the specific heat. Measurements made under constant atmospheric pressure give q_p = ΔH; those in a sealed bomb give q_V = ΔU. A temperature rise in the solution means the reaction released heat, so ΔH is negative. For an ideal gas the molar heat capacities at constant pressure and constant volume are related by Cp − Cv = R.
Given: m = 100 g; c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹; ΔT = 6.8 K; n(H⁺) = n(OH⁻) = 0.0500 mol.
Formula/Principle: q = mcΔT; ΔH = −q/n(H₂O).
Step 1: q = 100 × 4.18 × 6.8 = 2842 J ≈ 2.84 kJ.
Step 2: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O: 0.0500 mol water formed.
Step 3: ΔH = −2.84/0.0500 = −56.8 kJ mol⁻¹.
Why: The heat released warms the solution; dividing by moles of water formed gives the molar enthalpy, close to the value for any strong acid–strong base pair.
Why not the others: (A) Heat calculated wrongly and the cup is at constant pressure. (C) Only 0.0500 mol water forms. (D) Heat halved and sign wrong.
Key point: q = mcΔT; constant pressure ⇒ q_p = ΔH; exothermic ⇒ ΔH < 0.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: How the degree of ionisation and [H⁺] of a weak acid change on dilution (Ostwald's law), the common ion effect, and Ka·Kb = Kw for a conjugate pair
questions.question: Ethanoic acid has Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵. Which statement is correct?
options: A) Dilution from 0.10 M to 0.0010 M decreases the degree of ionisation and increases [H⁺]
B) Adding sodium ethanoate increases the degree of ionisation of the acid
C) The degree of ionisation is the same at all concentrations, because Ka is constant

D) By α ≈ √(Ka/c), α is about 1.3 % at 0.10 M and about 13 % at 0.0010 M, so dilution increases α tenfold even though [H⁺] = αc falls from 1.3 × 10⁻³ M to 1.3 × 10⁻⁴ M; adding sodium ethanoate suppresses ionisation (common ion effect); the ethanoate ion has Kb = Kw/Ka ≈ 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) α: 1.3 % → 13 %; [H⁺]: 1.3 × 10⁻³ → 1.3 × 10⁻⁴ M; common ion suppresses; Kb(CH₃COO⁻) ≈ 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰.
Concept: For a weak acid HA of concentration c and degree of ionisation α, Ka = cα²/(1 − α) ≈ cα² when α is small, so α ≈ √(Ka/c): α increases on dilution. The common ion effect is the shift in equilibrium on adding a substance that provides more of an ionic species already present in the dissociation equilibrium; adding acetate ions to acetic acid suppresses its ionisation. For a conjugate acid–base pair, Ka × Kb = Kw.
Given: Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵; c = 0.10 and 0.0010 M; Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴.
Formula/Principle: α = √(Ka/c); [H⁺] = αc = √(Ka c); Kb = Kw/Ka.
Step 1: c = 0.10: α = √(1.8 × 10⁻⁴) = 1.34 × 10⁻² (1.3 %); [H⁺] = 1.34 × 10⁻³ M.
Step 2: c = 0.0010: α = √(1.8 × 10⁻²) = 0.134 (13 %); [H⁺] = 1.34 × 10⁻⁴ M.
Step 3: Kb = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴/1.8 × 10⁻⁵ = 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰.
Why: Dilution spreads ions apart, making recombination less likely, so a larger fraction ionises; but the total acid present falls faster than α rises.
Why not the others: (A) Reversed effects. (B) A common ion suppresses ionisation. (C) α depends on concentration.
Key point: α ∝ 1/√c for a weak acid; [H⁺] ∝ √c; common ion suppresses α; KaKb = Kw.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Solving a sin x + cos x = k type equation by writing it as a single sine, the condition for solvability and the general solution
questions.question: For which real \(k\) does \(\sin x+\cos x=k\) have a real solution, and what is the general solution when \(k=1\)?
options: A) \(|k|\le\sqrt2\); for \(k=1\): \(x=2n\pi\) or \(x=2n\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\), \(n\in\mathbb Z\)
D) every real \(k\); for \(k=1\): \(x=\dfrac{n\pi}{2}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(|k|\le\sqrt2\); \(x=2n\pi\) or \(2n\pi+\frac{\pi}{2}\).
Given: \(\sin x+\cos x=k\)
Formula/Principle: \(a\sin x+b\cos x=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\,\sin(x+\alpha);\ \sin\theta=\sin\alpha\Rightarrow\theta=n\pi+(-1)^n\alpha\)
Step 1: \(\sin x+\cos x=\sqrt2\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\sin x+\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\cos x\right)=\sqrt2\sin\left(x+\tfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\)
Step 2: \(\text{since }|\sin|\le1,\ \text{a solution exists iff }|k|\le\sqrt2\)
Step 3: \(k=1:\ \sin\left(x+\tfrac{\pi}{4}\right)=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}=\sin\tfrac{\pi}{4}\Rightarrow x+\tfrac{\pi}{4}=n\pi+(-1)^n\tfrac{\pi}{4}\)
Worked derivation: \[n=2m:\ x=2m\pi;\qquad n=2m+1:\ x=(2m+1)\pi-\tfrac{\pi}{2}=2m\pi+\tfrac{\pi}{2}\]
Check: \[x=0:\ 0+1=1\ \checkmark;\quad x=\tfrac{\pi}{2}:\ 1+0=1\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{combining the two terms into one sine shows the expression ranges exactly over }[-\sqrt2,\sqrt2]\text{, and the general solution of a sine equation then follows}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{the amplitude is }\sqrt2\text{, and }x=\pi\text{ gives }-1\); (C) \(x=\tfrac{\pi}{4}\text{ gives }\sqrt2\neq1\); (D) \(k=2\text{ has no solution}\).
Key point: \(\sin x+\cos x\in[-\sqrt2,\sqrt2]\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the real values of a parameter for which both roots of a quadratic lie inside a given interval, by solving for the roots explicitly
questions.question: For which real \(k\) do both roots of \(x^2-2kx+k^2-4=0\) lie strictly between \(-3\) and \(5\)?
options: A) \(k>-1\) only
C) \(-1<k<3\); the integer values of \(k\) are \(0,1,2\)
D) every real \(k\), since the discriminant is always positive
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(-1<k<3\); integer values \(0,1,2\).
Given: \(x^2-2kx+k^2-4=0;\ \text{interval }(-3,5)\)
Formula/Principle: \(x^2-2kx+k^2-4=(x-k)^2-4\Rightarrow\text{roots }k\pm2\)
Step 1: \(\text{discriminant }4k^2-4(k^2-4)=16>0\Rightarrow\text{roots }k-2,\ k+2\text{ always real and distinct}\)
Step 2: \(\text{smaller root: }k-2>-3\Rightarrow k>-1\)
Step 3: \(\text{larger root: }k+2<5\Rightarrow k<3\Rightarrow-1<k<3\)
Worked derivation: \[k=0:\ \text{roots }\pm2\in(-3,5)\ \checkmark;\quad k=3:\ \text{roots }1,5\ (5\text{ not strictly inside})\]
Check: \[\text{general test: }f(-3)>0,\ f(5)>0,\ -3<k<5:\ (k+3)^2>4\text{ and }(k-5)^2>4\text{ give the same range}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{both roots lie in the interval only when the smaller exceeds the left end and the larger is below the right end}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{ignores the right end}\); (B) \(\text{puts the vertex, not both roots, in the interval}\); (D) \(\text{real roots need not lie in the interval}\).
Key point: \(\text{both roots in }(a,b)\Leftrightarrow\text{smaller root}>a\text{ and larger root}<b\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Arrangements of a word with repeated letters and the number in which two identical letters are not together
questions.question: How many arrangements of the letters of ARRANGE are there, and in how many are the two R's not together?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(1260\) arrangements; \(900\) with the R's apart.
Given: \(\text{ARRANGE: 7 letters, A twice, R twice, N, G, E once}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac{n!}{p!\,q!}\text{ for repeated letters; complement: apart}=\text{total}-\text{together}\)
Step 1: \(\text{total}=\dfrac{7!}{2!\,2!}=\dfrac{5040}{4}=1260\)
Step 2: \(\text{R's together: treat RR as one block}\Rightarrow 6\text{ objects with A twice: }\dfrac{6!}{2!}=360\)
Step 3: \(\text{apart}=1260-360=900\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{gap method: arrange A,A,N,G,E in }\tfrac{5!}{2!}=60\text{ ways; choose 2 of 6 gaps: }\binom62=15;\ 60\times15=900\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[900+360=1260\]
Why: \(\text{dividing by }2!\text{ for each repeated letter removes orderings that look identical; the complement handles "not together"}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{ignores repeats}\); (B) \(\text{divides by only one }2!\); (C) \(\text{360 is the "together" count}\).
Key point: \(\text{not together}=\text{total}-\text{together (block method)}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding two positive numbers from their arithmetic and geometric means, their harmonic mean and the relation G² = AH
questions.question: Two positive numbers have arithmetic mean 10 and geometric mean 8. What are the numbers and their harmonic mean?
options: A) 12 and 8; HM 9.6
B) 16 and 4; HM 6.4, and \(G^2=AH\) holds
C) 18 and 2; HM 3.6
D) 16 and 4; HM 10
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(16\) and \(4\); \(H=6.4\).
Given: \(A=\dfrac{a+b}{2}=10,\ G=\sqrt{ab}=8\)
Formula/Principle: \(a,b\text{ are roots of }x^2-2Ax+G^2=0;\ H=\dfrac{2ab}{a+b}=\dfrac{G^2}{A}\)
Step 1: \(a+b=20,\ ab=64\Rightarrow x^2-20x+64=0\)
Step 2: \((x-16)(x-4)=0\Rightarrow a=16,\ b=4\)
Step 3: \(H=\dfrac{2\cdot64}{20}=6.4\)
Worked derivation: \[G^2=64=10\times6.4=AH\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[A\ge G\ge H:\ 10\ge8\ge6.4\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the AM gives the sum and the GM gives the product, which fix the two numbers as roots of a quadratic}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\sqrt{96}\ne8\); (C) \(\sqrt{36}=6\ne8\); (D) \(\text{HM cannot exceed GM}\).
Key point: \(A\ge G\ge H,\ G^2=AH\text{ for two positive numbers}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the acute angle between two lines from their slopes using the tangent formula
questions.question: What is the acute angle between the lines \(y=2x+1\) and \(y=-3x+5\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(45^\circ\).
Given: \(m_1=2,\ m_2=-3\)
Formula/Principle: \(\tan\theta=\left|\dfrac{m_1-m_2}{1+m_1m_2}\right|\)
Step 1: \(m_1-m_2=2-(-3)=5\)
Step 2: \(1+m_1m_2=1-6=-5\)
Step 3: \(\tan\theta=|5/(-5)|=1\Rightarrow\theta=45^\circ\)
Worked derivation: \[\tan^{-1}2\approx63.43^\circ,\ \ \tan^{-1}(-3)\approx108.43^\circ;\ \ 108.43^\circ-63.43^\circ=45^\circ\]
Check: \[m_1m_2=-6\ne-1\Rightarrow\text{not perpendicular}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the angle between lines is the difference of their inclinations, and }\tan(\theta_2-\theta_1)\text{ expands to the formula}\)
Why not the others: (A),(B) \(\text{would need }\tan\theta=1/\sqrt3\text{ or }\sqrt3\); (C) \(\text{needs }m_1m_2=-1\).
Key point: \(\tan\theta=\left|\frac{m_1-m_2}{1+m_1m_2}\right|\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Completing squares to identify a second-degree equation as an ellipse, finding its centre, axes and eccentricity, and the degenerate cases
questions.question: By completing squares, identify the curve \(x^2+4y^2-2x+16y+13=0\) and give its centre, axes and eccentricity. Which description is correct?
options: A) a circle of radius 2 centred at \((1,-2)\)

B) the ellipse \(\dfrac{(x-1)^2}{4}+\dfrac{(y+2)^2}{1}=1\), centre \((1,-2)\), major axis 4, minor axis 2, eccentricity \(\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\); if the constant 13 were replaced by 17 the equation would represent only the point \((1,-2)\), and by any number above 17, no real points
C) a hyperbola centred at \((-1,2)\)
D) a parabola with vertex \((1,-2)\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Ellipse with centre \((1,-2)\), \(a=2,\ b=1,\ e=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\).
Given: \(x^2+4y^2-2x+16y+13=0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{complete squares; }\dfrac{(x-h)^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{(y-k)^2}{b^2}=1,\ e=\sqrt{1-b^2/a^2}\)
Step 1: \(x^2-2x=(x-1)^2-1;\quad 4y^2+16y=4(y+2)^2-16\)
Step 2: \((x-1)^2+4(y+2)^2-1-16+13=0\Rightarrow(x-1)^2+4(y+2)^2=4\)
Step 3: \(\text{divide by 4: }\dfrac{(x-1)^2}{4}+(y+2)^2=1\Rightarrow a=2,\ b=1\)
Worked derivation: \[e=\sqrt{1-\tfrac14}=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2};\quad\text{constant }c:\ (x-1)^2+4(y+2)^2=17-c\]
Check: \[(3,-2):\ 9+16-6-32+13=0\ \checkmark\ (\text{end of major axis})\]
Why: \(\text{both squared terms have positive but unequal coefficients, giving an ellipse once the right side is positive}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{unequal coefficients of }x^2,y^2\); (C) \(\text{needs opposite signs}\); (D) \(\text{both variables are squared}\).
Key point: \(\text{complete squares; right side }>0,=0,<0\Rightarrow\text{ellipse, point, empty}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding all circles that touch both coordinate axes and have their centre on a given line
questions.question: Which are all the circles that touch both coordinate axes and have their centres on the line \(2x-y=3\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \((x-3)^2+(y-3)^2=9\) and \((x-1)^2+(y+1)^2=1\).
Given: \(\text{centre }(h,k)\text{ on }2x-y=3;\ \text{touches both axes}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{touching both axes}\Rightarrow|h|=|k|=r\)
Step 1: \(k=h:\ 2h-h=3\Rightarrow h=3,\ k=3,\ r=3\)
Step 2: \(k=-h:\ 2h+h=3\Rightarrow h=1,\ k=-1,\ r=1\)
Step 3: \(\text{circles }(x-3)^2+(y-3)^2=9\text{ and }(x-1)^2+(y+1)^2=1\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{centres: }2(3)-3=3\ \checkmark;\quad2(1)-(-1)=3\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[\text{distance of }(1,-1)\text{ from each axis}=1=r\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a circle touching both axes has its centre on }y=x\text{ or }y=-x\text{, each meeting the given line once}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{misses the case }k=-h\); (C) \(2(-3)-(-3)=-3\ne3\); (D) \(\text{centres }(1,1),(3,-3)\text{ are not on the line}\).
Key point: \(\text{touching both axes}\Rightarrow\text{centre on }y=\pm x,\ r=|h|\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Evaluating three standard limits: a ratio of sines, an exponential limit and the limit of (1 − cos x)/x²
questions.question: What are the values of \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin3x}{\sin5x}\), \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{e^{8x}-1}{x}\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{1-\cos x}{x^2}\), in that order?
options: C) \(\tfrac35,\ 8,\ \tfrac12\)
D) \(\tfrac35,\ \tfrac18,\ 1\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\frac35,\ 8,\ \frac12\).
Given: \(\text{three limits as }x\to0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\lim\dfrac{\sin x}{x}=1;\ \lim\dfrac{e^x-1}{x}=1;\ 1-\cos x=2\sin^2\tfrac{x}{2}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{\sin3x}{\sin5x}=\dfrac{\sin3x}{3x}\cdot\dfrac{5x}{\sin5x}\cdot\dfrac35\to\dfrac35\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{e^{8x}-1}{x}=8\cdot\dfrac{e^{8x}-1}{8x}\to8\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{1-\cos x}{x^2}=\dfrac{2\sin^2(x/2)}{x^2}=\dfrac12\left(\dfrac{\sin(x/2)}{x/2}\right)^2\to\dfrac12\)
Worked derivation: \[x=0.01:\ \frac{1-\cos0.01}{10^{-4}}\approx\frac{5.0\times10^{-5}}{10^{-4}}=0.5\]
Check: \[\text{series }1-\cos x\approx\tfrac{x^2}{2}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{each limit is rescaled to a standard form whose value is 1, and the leftover constant gives the answer}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{ratio inverted; third limit wrong}\); (B) \(\text{ignores the multipliers}\); (D) \(\text{second limit inverted}\).
Key point: \(\frac{\sin ax}{\sin bx}\to\frac ab;\ \frac{e^{ax}-1}{x}\to a;\ \frac{1-\cos x}{x^2}\to\frac12\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Bayes' theorem for a student who either knows the answer or guesses among four options, given that the answer is correct
questions.question: In a four-option MCQ, a student knows the answer with probability \(\tfrac34\) and otherwise guesses at random. Given that the student answered correctly, what is the probability that the student knew the answer?
options: A) \(\tfrac34\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\frac{12}{13}\).
Given: \(P(K)=\tfrac34,\ P(G)=\tfrac14,\ P(C\mid K)=1,\ P(C\mid G)=\tfrac14\)
Formula/Principle: \(P(K\mid C)=\dfrac{P(K)P(C\mid K)}{P(K)P(C\mid K)+P(G)P(C\mid G)}\)
Step 1: \(P(K)P(C\mid K)=\tfrac34\)
Step 2: \(P(G)P(C\mid G)=\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac14=\tfrac1{16}\)
Step 3: \(P(C)=\tfrac{12}{16}+\tfrac{1}{16}=\tfrac{13}{16}\Rightarrow P(K\mid C)=\dfrac{12/16}{13/16}=\tfrac{12}{13}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{out of 64 students: 48 know (all correct), 16 guess (4 correct)}\Rightarrow\tfrac{48}{52}=\tfrac{12}{13}\]
Check: \[P(G\mid C)=\tfrac1{13};\ \tfrac{12}{13}+\tfrac1{13}=1\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a correct answer is evidence of knowing, so the posterior }\tfrac{12}{13}\text{ exceeds the prior }\tfrac34\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{the prior, ignores the evidence}\); (B) \(\text{that is }P(C)\); (D) \(\text{that is }P(G\mid C)\).
Key point: \(\text{posterior}=\frac{\text{prior}\times\text{likelihood}}{\text{total probability}}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Solving an equation in inverse tangents using the addition formula and rejecting the extraneous root
questions.question: Which value(s) of \(x\) satisfy \(\tan^{-1}x+\tan^{-1}2x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\)?
options: A) only \(x=\dfrac{-3+\sqrt{17}}{4}\)
C) only \(x=\dfrac{-3-\sqrt{17}}{4}\)
D) \(x=\dfrac13\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(x=\frac{-3+\sqrt{17}}{4}\approx0.281\).
Given: \(\tan^{-1}x+\tan^{-1}2x=\tfrac{\pi}{4}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\tan^{-1}a+\tan^{-1}b=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{a+b}{1-ab}\ (ab<1)\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{3x}{1-2x^2}=1\Rightarrow2x^2+3x-1=0\)
Step 2: \(x=\dfrac{-3\pm\sqrt{9+8}}{4}=\dfrac{-3\pm\sqrt{17}}{4}\)
Step 3: \(\text{the negative root }\approx-1.78\text{ makes both terms negative, so the sum cannot be }\tfrac{\pi}{4}\text{; reject}\)
Worked derivation: \[x\approx0.281:\ \tan^{-1}0.281+\tan^{-1}0.562\approx15.7^\circ+29.3^\circ=45^\circ\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[x\approx-1.78:\ \tan^{-1}(-1.78)+\tan^{-1}(-3.56)\approx-60.7^\circ-74.3^\circ=-135^\circ\ne45^\circ\]
Why: \(\text{taking tangents of both sides can introduce roots where the true sum is }\tfrac{\pi}{4}-\pi\text{, so each root must be checked}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{includes the extraneous root}\); (C) \(\text{keeps the wrong root}\); (D) \(\tan^{-1}\tfrac13+\tan^{-1}\tfrac23\ne\tfrac{\pi}{4}\ (\tfrac{1}{1-2/9}=\tfrac97)\).
Key point: \(\text{always check roots of inverse-trig equations against the principal ranges}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Area of a triangle from coordinates with an unknown vertex, the values giving a given area and the collinearity condition
questions.question: The triangle with vertices \((1,2)\), \((4,6)\) and \((k,0)\) has area 7 square units. Which statement is correct?
options: A) \(k=3\) only
B) \(k=-3\) or \(k=4\); collinear when \(k=\tfrac12\)
D) the area equals \(|1+2k|\), so \(k=3\) or \(k=-4\); the three points are collinear when \(k=-\tfrac12\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Area \(=|1+2k|\); \(k=3\) or \(-4\); collinear at \(k=-\frac12\).
Given: \((x_1,y_1)=(1,2),\ (x_2,y_2)=(4,6),\ (x_3,y_3)=(k,0)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\Delta=\tfrac12\left|x_1(y_2-y_3)+x_2(y_3-y_1)+x_3(y_1-y_2)\right|\)
Step 1: \(\Delta=\tfrac12|1(6)+4(-2)+k(-4)|=\tfrac12|-2-4k|=|1+2k|\)
Step 2: \(|1+2k|=7\Rightarrow1+2k=7\text{ or }-7\Rightarrow k=3\text{ or }-4\)
Step 3: \(\text{collinear}\Leftrightarrow\Delta=0\Rightarrow k=-\tfrac12\)
Worked derivation: \[k=3:\ \tfrac12|6-8-12|=7\ \checkmark;\quad k=-4:\ \tfrac12|6-8+16|=7\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[\text{line through }(1,2),(4,6):\ y-2=\tfrac43(x-1);\ y=0\Rightarrow x=-\tfrac12\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the absolute value makes the area equation give two positions, one on each side of the line through the fixed vertices}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{misses the second sign}\); (B) \(\text{sign errors}\); (C) \(\text{forgets the factor of 2 in }1+2k\).
Key point: \(\text{area }=\tfrac12|\det|\text{; area }0\Leftrightarrow\text{collinear}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Implicit differentiation of x² + xy + y² = 7 at a point, and the slope of a parametric curve checked against its Cartesian equation
questions.question: For the curve \(x^2+xy+y^2=7\), what is \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) at \((1,2)\)? And for the curve \(x=t+\dfrac1t,\ y=t-\dfrac1t\), what is \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) at \(t=2\)?
options: B) \(-\tfrac45\); \(\tfrac53\), and the curve is the hyperbola \(x^2-y^2=4\)
C) \(\tfrac45\); \(\tfrac53\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(-\frac45\); \(\frac53\).
Given: \(x^2+xy+y^2=7\text{ through }(1,2);\ x=t+\tfrac1t,\ y=t-\tfrac1t,\ t=2\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{implicit: differentiate term by term, product rule on }xy;\ \text{parametric: }\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}\)
Step 1: \(2x+y+xy'+2yy'=0\Rightarrow y'=-\dfrac{2x+y}{x+2y}=-\dfrac45\text{ at }(1,2)\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{dx}{dt}=1-\dfrac1{t^2},\ \dfrac{dy}{dt}=1+\dfrac1{t^2}\Rightarrow\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{t^2+1}{t^2-1}\)
Step 3: \(t=2:\ \dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{5}{3}\)
Worked derivation: \[x^2-y^2=\left(t+\tfrac1t\right)^2-\left(t-\tfrac1t\right)^2=4;\quad 2x-2yy'=0\Rightarrow y'=\frac xy=\frac{5/2}{3/2}=\frac53\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[(1,2):\ 1+2+4=7\ \checkmark;\quad t=2\Rightarrow(x,y)=(2.5,1.5)\]
Why: \(\text{implicit differentiation treats }y\text{ as a function of }x\text{; for a parametric curve the chain rule divides the two rates}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{both slopes inverted}\); (C) \(\text{sign of the first slope wrong}\); (D) \(\text{arithmetic errors}\).
Key point: \(y'=-\frac{F_x}{F_y};\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{\dot y}{\dot x}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Maximising the area of a rectangular field along a river with a fixed length of fence on three sides, and the widths that give a smaller area
questions.question: A farmer has 120 m of fence to enclose a rectangular field beside a straight river (no fence along the river). What is the largest possible area, and for which widths \(x\) (the sides perpendicular to the river) is the area 1600 m²?
options: D) \(1800\ \text{m}^2\) at \(x=60\) m; no width gives 1600 m²
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(1800\ \text{m}^2\) at \(x=30\); \(1600\ \text{m}^2\) at \(x=20\) or \(40\).
Given: \(\text{fence: }2x+y=120;\ \text{area }A=xy\)
Formula/Principle: \(A(x)=x(120-2x);\ A'(x)=0,\ A''<0\Rightarrow\text{max}\)
Step 1: \(A=120x-2x^2;\ A'=120-4x=0\Rightarrow x=30\)
Step 2: \(A''=-4<0\Rightarrow\text{max};\ y=60,\ A=1800\ \text{m}^2\)
Step 3: \(120x-2x^2=1600\Rightarrow x^2-60x+800=0\Rightarrow(x-20)(x-40)=0\)
Worked derivation: \[x=20:\ y=80,\ A=1600\ \checkmark;\quad x=40:\ y=40,\ A=1600\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[\text{the parabola }A(x)\text{ is symmetric about }x=30:\ 20\text{ and }40\text{ are equidistant}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the area is a downward parabola in }x\text{; any value below the maximum is reached at two widths symmetric about the vertex}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{that is a square with fence on 4 sides}\); (C) \(\text{needs }y=90\text{ with }x=40\text{, exceeding the fence}\); (D) \(x=60\text{ leaves }y=0\).
Key point: \(A=x(L-2x)\text{ is maximum at }x=L/4\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Partial fractions with a parameter in the numerator and the value of the parameter that removes one logarithm from the integral
questions.question: Write \(\dfrac{x+k}{(x-1)(x+2)}=\dfrac{A}{x-1}+\dfrac{B}{x+2}\). Which statement is correct?
options: A) \(A=\dfrac{k}{3},\ B=\dfrac{1}{3}\); the integral never contains \(\ln|x-1|\)
B) \(A=1,\ B=k\) for all \(k\)
C) \(A=\dfrac{2-k}{3},\ B=\dfrac{1+k}{3}\); \(\ln|x+2|\) disappears when \(k=2\)
D) \(A=\dfrac{1+k}{3},\ B=\dfrac{2-k}{3}\); the integral \(\displaystyle\int\frac{x+k}{(x-1)(x+2)}dx\) has no \(\ln|x-1|\) term exactly when \(k=-1\), and then equals \(\ln|x+2|+C\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(A=\frac{1+k}{3},\ B=\frac{2-k}{3}\); \(k=-1\) removes \(\ln|x-1|\).
Given: \(x+k=A(x+2)+B(x-1)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{cover-up: put }x=1\text{ and }x=-2\)
Step 1: \(x=1:\ 1+k=3A\Rightarrow A=\dfrac{1+k}{3}\)
Step 2: \(x=-2:\ -2+k=-3B\Rightarrow B=\dfrac{2-k}{3}\)
Step 3: \(\displaystyle\int=A\ln|x-1|+B\ln|x+2|+C;\ A=0\Leftrightarrow k=-1\)
Worked derivation: \[k=-1:\ \frac{x-1}{(x-1)(x+2)}=\frac{1}{x+2}\Rightarrow\int=\ln|x+2|+C;\ B=\tfrac{3}{3}=1\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[A+B=\tfrac{1+k+2-k}{3}=1=\text{coefficient of }x\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a logarithm term vanishes when the numerator shares the corresponding factor of the denominator}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(A\text{ and }B\text{ wrong}\); (B) \(\text{fails }A+B=1\text{ unless }k=0\); (C) \(A\text{ and }B\text{ swapped}\).
Key point: \(\text{cover-up rule; a factor cancelling the numerator removes its log}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Integrating x sin nx over [0, π] by parts and determining its sign for positive integers n
questions.question: Let \(I_n=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}x\sin nx\,dx\) for positive integers \(n\). How many of \(I_1,I_2,\dots,I_6\) are positive?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(3\) (\(n=1,3,5\)).
Given: \(I_n=\int_0^\pi x\sin nx\,dx,\ n\in\{1,\dots,6\}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\int u\,dv=uv-\int v\,du\text{ with }u=x,\ dv=\sin nx\,dx\)
Step 1: \(I_n=\left[-\dfrac{x\cos nx}{n}\right]_0^\pi+\dfrac1n\int_0^\pi\cos nx\,dx\)
Step 2: \(\int_0^\pi\cos nx\,dx=\left[\dfrac{\sin nx}{n}\right]_0^\pi=0\)
Step 3: \(I_n=-\dfrac{\pi\cos n\pi}{n}=\dfrac{\pi(-1)^{n+1}}{n}\Rightarrow\text{positive for odd }n\)
Worked derivation: \[I_1=\pi,\ I_2=-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\ I_3=\tfrac{\pi}{3},\ I_4=-\tfrac{\pi}{4},\ I_5=\tfrac{\pi}{5},\ I_6=-\tfrac{\pi}{6}\]
Check: \[n=1:\ x\sin x\ge0\text{ on }[0,\pi]\Rightarrow I_1>0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{for even }n\text{ the negative lobes of }\sin nx\text{ lie at larger }x\text{, where the weight }x\text{ is bigger, so they win}\)
Why not the others: (A),(B),(D) \(\text{the sign alternates with }n\text{, giving three positive values}\).
Key point: \(\int_0^\pi x\sin nx\,dx=\frac{\pi(-1)^{n+1}}{n}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Solving the linear differential equation y′ + y = x with an initial condition and analysing the solution's minimum and slant asymptote
questions.question: The solution of \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}+y=x\) with \(y(0)=1\) is \(y(x)\). Which statement is correct?
options: A) \(y=x-1+2e^{-x}\); its minimum is at \(x=\ln2\) with value \(\ln2\), and \(y\to x-1\) as \(x\to\infty\)
B) \(y=x+e^{-x}\); minimum at \(x=0\)
C) \(y=x-1+e^{x}\); no minimum
D) \(y=2e^{-x}-x\); decreasing everywhere
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(y=x-1+2e^{-x}\); minimum \(\ln2\) at \(x=\ln2\); asymptote \(y=x-1\).
Given: \(y'+y=x,\ y(0)=1\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{I.F.}=e^{\int1\,dx}=e^x;\ \ y\,e^x=\int x e^x\,dx\)
Step 1: \(\int xe^x\,dx=(x-1)e^x+C\Rightarrow y=x-1+Ce^{-x}\)
Step 2: \(y(0)=-1+C=1\Rightarrow C=2\)
Step 3: \(y'=1-2e^{-x}=0\Rightarrow x=\ln2;\ y''=2e^{-x}>0\Rightarrow\text{minimum}\)
Worked derivation: \[y(\ln2)=\ln2-1+2\cdot\tfrac12=\ln2\approx0.693\]
Check: \[y'+y=(1-2e^{-x})+(x-1+2e^{-x})=x\ \checkmark;\quad y(0)=-1+2=1\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the integrating factor makes the left side an exact derivative; the decaying term }2e^{-x}\text{ dies out, leaving the line }x-1\)
Why not the others: (B) \(y'+y=1+x\ne x\); (C) \(\text{the exponential should decay}\); (D) \(\text{fails the equation}\).
Key point: \(y'+Py=Q\Rightarrow y\,e^{\int P}=\int Qe^{\int P}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Section formula in three dimensions for internal and external division, direction cosines of a segment and counting lattice points on it
questions.question: For \(A(1,2,3)\) and \(B(4,8,9)\), which statement is correct?
options: A) the segment \(AB\) contains 4 points with integer coordinates (including \(A\) and \(B\)); the point dividing \(AB\) internally in the ratio \(1:2\) is \((2,4,5)\), externally in \(1:2\) is \((-2,-4,-3)\); the direction cosines of \(\vec{AB}\) are \(\left(\tfrac13,\tfrac23,\tfrac23\right)\)
B) \(AB\) contains 10 lattice points; internal \(1:2\) point \((3,6,7)\)
C) internal \(1:2\) point \((2,4,5)\); external \(1:2\) point \((7,14,15)\); direction cosines \((3,6,6)\)
D) direction cosines \(\left(\tfrac19,\tfrac29,\tfrac29\right)\); 2 lattice points
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(4\) lattice points; \((2,4,5)\); \((-2,-4,-3)\); \(\left(\frac13,\frac23,\frac23\right)\).
Given: \(\vec{AB}=(3,6,6),\ |AB|=\sqrt{9+36+36}=9\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{internal }m:n:\ \dfrac{mB+nA}{m+n};\ \text{external: }\dfrac{mB-nA}{m-n};\ \text{lattice points}=\gcd(3,6,6)+1\)
Step 1: \(\text{internal }1:2:\ \dfrac{(4,8,9)+2(1,2,3)}{3}=\dfrac{(6,12,15)}{3}=(2,4,5)\)
Step 2: \(\text{external }1:2:\ \dfrac{(4,8,9)-2(1,2,3)}{-1}=-(2,4,3)=(-2,-4,-3)\)
Step 3: \(\gcd=3\Rightarrow A+t(1,2,2),\ t=0,1,2,3:\ 4\text{ lattice points}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{d.c.}=\tfrac{(3,6,6)}{9}=\left(\tfrac13,\tfrac23,\tfrac23\right);\ \tfrac19+\tfrac49+\tfrac49=1\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[AP=|(1,2,2)|=3,\ PB=|(2,4,4)|=6\Rightarrow1:2\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the section formula weights each end by the opposite ratio part; the gcd of the coordinate differences counts equal integer steps}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{wrong lattice count and point}\); (C) \(\text{external formula misapplied; direction ratios are not cosines}\); (D) \(\text{divides by 27 instead of 9}\).
Key point: \(\text{d.c.}=\frac{\text{d.r.}}{\text{length}};\ \text{lattice points on segment}=\gcd+1\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Shortest distance between two lines in vector form with a parameter, the condition for them to intersect and the angle between them
questions.question: \(L_1:\ \vec r=(1,2,1)+\lambda(1,-1,1)\) and \(L_2:\ \vec r=(2,k,3)+\mu(2,1,-1)\). Which statement is correct?
options: A) the shortest distance is \(|k|\) and the lines are parallel
B) the lines intersect for every \(k\)
C) the shortest distance is \(\dfrac{|k-2|}{\sqrt2}\); the lines meet at \(60^\circ\)
D) the shortest distance is \(\dfrac{|k|}{\sqrt2}\), so the lines intersect only when \(k=0\); they are perpendicular, since \((1,-1,1)\cdot(2,1,-1)=0\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(d=\frac{|k|}{\sqrt2}\); intersect iff \(k=0\); perpendicular.
Given: \(\vec a_1=(1,2,1),\ \vec b_1=(1,-1,1);\ \vec a_2=(2,k,3),\ \vec b_2=(2,1,-1)\)
Formula/Principle: \(d=\dfrac{|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)|}{|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|}\)
Step 1: \(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2=\big((-1)(-1)-(1)(1),\ (1)(2)-(1)(-1),\ (1)(1)-(-1)(2)\big)=(0,3,3)\)
Step 2: \(\vec a_2-\vec a_1=(1,k-2,2);\ \text{dot}=0+3(k-2)+6=3k\)
Step 3: \(d=\dfrac{|3k|}{3\sqrt2}=\dfrac{|k|}{\sqrt2}\)
Worked derivation: \[k=0:\ (1+\lambda,2-\lambda,1+\lambda)=(2+2\mu,\mu,3-\mu)\Rightarrow\lambda=\tfrac43,\ \mu=\tfrac23:\ (\tfrac73,\tfrac23,\tfrac73)\ \text{on both}\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[\vec b_1\cdot\vec b_2=2-1-1=0\Rightarrow90^\circ\]
Why: \(\text{the shortest distance is the projection of the joining vector on the common normal; it is zero exactly when the lines meet}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{direction vectors are not parallel}\); (B) \(d\ne0\text{ for }k\ne0\); (C) \(\text{wrong dot product and angle}\).
Key point: \(\text{coplanar/intersecting}\Leftrightarrow(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)=0\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Counting all functions, one-one functions and onto functions between finite sets, and checking a real function for bijectivity
questions.question: Which statement about functions is correct?
options: A) From a 3-element set to a 4-element set there are 12 functions, of which 24 are one-one; \(f(x)=x^3+x\) on \(\mathbb R\) is not one-one
B) From a 4-element set onto a 3-element set there are 81 functions

C) From \(\{1,2,3\}\) to \(\{a,b,c,d\}\) there are \(4^3=64\) functions, of which \(4\cdot3\cdot2=24\) are one-one; from a 4-element set to a 3-element set there are \(3^4-3\cdot2^4+3=36\) onto functions; \(f(x)=x^3+x\) is a bijection of \(\mathbb R\) onto \(\mathbb R\)
D) There are no onto functions from a 4-element set to a 3-element set
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(64\) functions, \(24\) one-one; \(36\) onto; \(x^3+x\) bijective.
Given: \(|A|=3,\ |B|=4;\ \text{onto from 4 to 3 elements}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{functions }|B|^{|A|};\ \text{one-one }{}^{|B|}P_{|A|};\ \text{onto by inclusion–exclusion}\)
Step 1: \(4^3=64;\ \ 4\times3\times2=24\)
Step 2: \(\text{onto}=3^4-\binom31 2^4+\binom32 1^4=81-48+3=36\)
Step 3: \(f'(x)=3x^2+1>0\Rightarrow\text{strictly increasing (one-one)};\ f\to\pm\infty\text{ and continuous}\Rightarrow\text{onto}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{onto check: choose the pair sharing an image }\binom42=6,\ \text{assign 3 blocks to 3 images }3!=6:\ 6\times6=36\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[36\le81\text{ (all functions from 4 to 3)}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{inclusion–exclusion removes functions that miss one or more elements of the codomain}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{counts reversed; }x^3+x\text{ is one-one}\); (B) \(81\text{ is all functions}\); (D) \(\text{36 exist}\).
Key point: \(\text{onto}(n\to3)=3^n-3\cdot2^n+3\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Solving Cauchy's functional equation for a continuous function, and counting the self-inverse functions on a three-element set
questions.question: \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is continuous, \(f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)\) for all \(x,y\), and \(f(1)=3\). Also, let \(N\) be the number of functions \(g:\{1,2,3\}\to\{1,2,3\}\) with \(g(g(x))=x\) for all \(x\). Which is correct?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(f(x)=3x\); \(N=4\).
Given: \(f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y),\ f\text{ continuous},\ f(1)=3\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{additivity}\Rightarrow f(q)=qf(1)\text{ for rational }q;\ \text{continuity extends to all reals}\)
Step 1: \(x=y=0:\ f(0)=2f(0)\Rightarrow f(0)=0;\ f(n)=nf(1)=3n\)
Step 2: \(nf(1/n)=f(1)\Rightarrow f(m/n)=3m/n;\ \text{rationals are dense and }f\text{ continuous}\Rightarrow f(x)=3x\)
Step 3: \(g\circ g=\text{id}\Rightarrow g\text{ is a bijection made of fixed points and swaps: identity, }(12),(13),(23)\Rightarrow N=4\)
Worked derivation: \[3(x+y)=3x+3y\ \checkmark;\ f(1)=3\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[3\text{-cycles fail: }g=(123)\Rightarrow g(g(1))=3\ne1\]
Why: \(\text{an additive function is linear on rationals, and continuity forces the same line everywhere; an involution can only fix or swap elements}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(3^{x+y}\ne3^x+3^y\text{; 6 counts all bijections}\); (C) \(f(0)\ne0\); (D) \(27\text{ counts all functions}\).
Key point: \(\text{continuous additive}\Rightarrow f(x)=cx;\ \text{involutions on 3 elements}=4\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Using Gauss's law with suitable Gaussian surfaces to find the fields of an infinite line charge, an infinite plane sheet and a thin spherical shell, and how each falls with distance
questions.question: Gauss's law gives the electric fields of three symmetric charge distributions. Which set of results is correct?
options: A) Line charge: \(E\propto\dfrac{1}{r^2}\); plane sheet: \(E\propto\dfrac1r\); shell: \(E\) inside equals \(\dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0R^2}\)
B) All three fields fall off as \(\dfrac{1}{r^2}\), because Coulomb's law is an inverse-square law
C) Plane sheet: \(E=\dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\) on each side; shell: \(E\) is maximum at the centre

D) Infinite line charge: \(E=\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0r}\) (cylindrical Gaussian surface); infinite plane sheet: \(E=\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\), independent of distance (pill-box surface); thin spherical shell: \(E=\dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2}\) outside (\(r>R\)) and \(E=0\) everywhere inside, because a concentric Gaussian sphere inside encloses no charge
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0r}\); \(\frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\); \(\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2}\) outside, \(0\) inside.
Given: \(\text{linear density }\lambda,\ \text{surface density }\sigma,\ \text{shell charge }Q\text{ and radius }R\)
Formula/Principle: \(\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec A=\dfrac{q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_0}\)
Step 1: \(\text{line: cylinder of radius }r,\ \text{length }l:\ E(2\pi rl)=\dfrac{\lambda l}{\varepsilon_0}\Rightarrow E=\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0r}\)
Step 2: \(\text{sheet: pill-box of face area }A:\ 2EA=\dfrac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_0}\Rightarrow E=\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\)
Step 3: \(\text{shell: sphere of radius }r:\ E(4\pi r^2)=\dfrac{Q}{\varepsilon_0}\ (r>R),\ =0\ (r<R)\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{line: }E\propto r^{-1};\quad\text{sheet: }E\propto r^{0};\quad\text{shell (outside): }E\propto r^{-2}\]
Check: \[\text{units: }\frac{\text{C/m}}{(\text{C}^2/\text{N m}^2)\,\text{m}}=\text{N/C}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the symmetry fixes the direction and makes }E\text{ constant on the Gaussian surface, so the flux integral becomes }E\times\text{area}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{powers mixed up; field inside a shell is zero}\); (B) \(\text{extended distributions change the distance dependence}\); (C) \(\sigma/\varepsilon_0\text{ is for a conductor's surface; field inside the shell is zero}\).
Key point: \(\text{line }1/r,\ \text{sheet constant},\ \text{shell }1/r^2\text{ outside and }0\text{ inside}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Effect of inserting an uncharged metal slab between capacitor plates connected to a battery on capacitance, charge, stored energy and the field in the gap
questions.question: An air-filled parallel-plate capacitor has plate area \(0.020\ \mathrm{m^2}\) and separation 5.0 mm, and is kept connected to a 100 V battery. An uncharged metal slab 3.0 mm thick, with the same area, is slid in parallel to the plates. Which result is correct (\(\varepsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{F/m}\))?
options: A) The capacitance rises from 35.4 pF to 88.5 pF; the charge rises from 3.54 nC to 8.85 nC; the stored energy rises from 0.177 µJ to 0.443 µJ; the field in each air gap becomes \(5.0\times10^4\ \mathrm{V/m}\), while the field inside the metal is zero
B) The capacitance falls to 14.2 pF, because metal blocks the field
C) The capacitance becomes infinite, because metal has infinite dielectric constant across the whole gap
D) The charge stays at 3.54 nC and the voltage falls to 40 V
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(35.4\to88.5\) pF; \(3.54\to8.85\) nC; \(0.177\to0.443\) µJ; gap field \(5.0\times10^4\) V/m.
Given: \(A=0.020\ \mathrm{m^2},\ d=5.0\ \mathrm{mm},\ t=3.0\ \mathrm{mm},\ V=100\ \mathrm{V}\text{ (battery connected)}\)
Formula/Principle: \(C_0=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d};\ \text{with a metal slab }C=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d-t};\ Q=CV;\ U=\tfrac12CV^2\)
Step 1: \(C_0=\dfrac{8.85\times10^{-12}\times0.020}{5.0\times10^{-3}}=3.54\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm F=35.4\ \mathrm{pF}\)
Step 2: \(C=\dfrac{8.85\times10^{-12}\times0.020}{2.0\times10^{-3}}=88.5\ \mathrm{pF}=2.5C_0\)
Step 3: \(Q_0=3.54\ \mathrm{nC}\to Q=8.85\ \mathrm{nC};\ U_0=\tfrac12(35.4\times10^{-12})(10^4)=1.77\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm J\to U=4.43\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm J\)
Worked derivation: \[E_{\text{gap}}=\frac{V}{d-t}=\frac{100}{2.0\times10^{-3}}=5.0\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{V/m};\quad E_{\text{metal}}=0\]
Check: \[\frac{Q}{\varepsilon_0A}=\frac{8.85\times10^{-9}}{1.77\times10^{-13}}=5.0\times10^4\ \mathrm{V/m}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{induced charges on the slab faces cancel the field inside it, so the whole voltage drops across the remaining 2 mm of air, as if the plates were closer}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{the slab increases }C\); (C) \(\text{only a slab filling the whole gap would short the plates}\); (D) \(\text{with the battery connected, }V\text{ stays 100 V and }Q\text{ changes}\).
Key point: \(\text{metal slab of thickness }t:\ C=\frac{\varepsilon_0A}{d-t}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Combining a metal resistor and a carbon resistor in series so that the total resistance does not change with temperature, and why the temperature coefficients have opposite signs
questions.question: A copper coil has resistance 10.0 Ω at 0 °C and temperature coefficient \(4.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}\). Carbon has temperature coefficient \(-5.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}\). What carbon resistance (at 0 °C) in series makes the total resistance nearly independent of temperature, and why?
options: A) 10 Ω; total 20 Ω, because equal resistances cancel

B) 80 Ω; total 90 Ω; the copper gains \(0.040\ \Omega\) per kelvin while the carbon loses \(80\times5\times10^{-4}=0.040\ \Omega\) per kelvin; resistance of a metal rises with temperature because the relaxation time of electrons falls (more collisions), while in carbon and semiconductors the number of charge carriers rises with temperature
C) 8.0 Ω; total 18 Ω
D) No combination can work, because both resistances increase with temperature
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(80\ \Omega\) of carbon; total \(90\ \Omega\).
Given: \(R_{\text{Cu}}=10.0\ \Omega,\ \alpha_{\text{Cu}}=4.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}};\ \alpha_{\text C}=-5.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}\)
Formula/Principle: \(R_T=R_0(1+\alpha\Delta T)\Rightarrow\dfrac{dR}{dT}=R_0\alpha;\ \text{series: }\dfrac{dR_{\text{tot}}}{dT}=R_{0,\text{Cu}}\alpha_{\text{Cu}}+R_{0,\text C}\alpha_{\text C}\)
Step 1: \(R_{0,\text{Cu}}\alpha_{\text{Cu}}=10\times4\times10^{-3}=0.040\ \Omega/\mathrm K\)
Step 2: \(R_{0,\text C}(-5\times10^{-4})=-0.040\Rightarrow R_{0,\text C}=80\ \Omega\)
Step 3: \(R_{\text{tot}}=10+80=90\ \Omega\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{at }50^\circ\mathrm C:\ R_{\text{Cu}}=10(1.20)=12.0,\ R_{\text C}=80(1-0.025)=78.0;\ \text{sum }90.0\ \Omega\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[\text{units: }\Omega\times\mathrm K^{-1}\ \text{on both sides}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\rho=\dfrac{m}{ne^2\tau}\text{: in metals }n\text{ is fixed and }\tau\text{ falls as }T\text{ rises; in carbon/semiconductors }n\text{ rises steeply, outweighing the fall in }\tau\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{the coefficients differ, so equal resistances do not cancel}\); (C) \(\text{gives only }-0.004\ \Omega/\mathrm K\); (D) \(\text{carbon's resistance falls with temperature}\).
Key point: \(\text{series compensation: }R_1\alpha_1+R_2\alpha_2=0\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Selecting proton speed with crossed electric and magnetic fields, then finding the radius and period of its circular path when only the magnetic field acts
questions.question: Protons pass undeflected through crossed fields \(E=3.0\times10^4\ \mathrm{V/m}\) and \(B=0.10\ \mathrm T\), then enter a region with only the same \(B\) (perpendicular to their velocity). What are their speed, orbit radius and period? (\(m_p=1.67\times10^{-27}\) kg, \(e=1.6\times10^{-19}\) C)
options: C) \(3.0\times10^5\ \mathrm{m/s}\); 3.13 cm; \(6.56\times10^{-7}\) s, the period being independent of the speed
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(v=3.0\times10^5\) m/s; \(r=3.13\) cm; \(T=6.56\times10^{-7}\) s.
Given: \(E=3.0\times10^4\ \mathrm{V/m},\ B=0.10\ \mathrm T,\ m=1.67\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg},\ q=1.6\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm C\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{undeflected: }qE=qvB\Rightarrow v=\dfrac EB;\ r=\dfrac{mv}{qB};\ T=\dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}\)
Step 1: \(v=\dfrac{3.0\times10^4}{0.10}=3.0\times10^5\ \mathrm{m/s}\)
Step 2: \(r=\dfrac{1.67\times10^{-27}\times3.0\times10^5}{1.6\times10^{-19}\times0.10}=\dfrac{5.01\times10^{-22}}{1.6\times10^{-20}}=3.13\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm m\)
Step 3: \(T=\dfrac{2\pi\times1.67\times10^{-27}}{1.6\times10^{-20}}=6.56\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm s\)
Worked derivation: \[T=\frac{2\pi r}{v}=\frac{2\pi\times0.0313}{3.0\times10^5}=6.56\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm s\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[\text{units: }\frac{\mathrm{kg\,m/s}}{\mathrm{C\,T}}=\frac{\mathrm{kg\,m/s}}{\mathrm{kg/s}}=\mathrm m\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{only particles with }v=E/B\text{ feel balanced forces; in the pure magnetic field the force is perpendicular to }v\text{, giving uniform circular motion}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{radius and period off by }10^2\); (B) \(\text{speed wrong}\); (D) \(\text{uses }B/E\).
Key point: \(v=E/B;\ r=mv/qB;\ T=2\pi m/qB\text{ (speed-independent)}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Measuring the speed of electromagnetic waves from the spacing of melted spots in a microwave oven with the turntable removed, using the standing-wave pattern
questions.question: With the turntable removed, a plate of cheese is heated briefly in a 2.45 GHz microwave oven. Melted spots appear in a line with a spacing of 6.1 cm. What does this give for the speed of the microwaves, and why?
options: A) \(1.5\times10^8\ \mathrm{m/s}\), because the spot spacing equals one wavelength

B) \(3.0\times10^8\ \mathrm{m/s}\): reflections from the metal walls set up a standing wave whose antinodes (hottest spots) are \(\lambda/2\) apart, so \(\lambda=12.2\) cm and \(c=f\lambda=2.45\times10^9\times0.122\approx2.99\times10^8\ \mathrm{m/s}\)
C) \(6.0\times10^8\ \mathrm{m/s}\), because the spots are a quarter-wavelength apart
D) \(3.4\times10^2\ \mathrm{m/s}\), because microwaves are sound waves in the oven's air
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\lambda=12.2\) cm; \(c\approx3.0\times10^8\) m/s.
Given: \(f=2.45\times10^9\ \mathrm{Hz};\ \text{spot spacing}=6.1\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{adjacent antinodes of a standing wave are }\lambda/2\text{ apart};\ c=f\lambda\)
Step 1: \(\lambda/2=6.1\ \mathrm{cm}\Rightarrow\lambda=12.2\ \mathrm{cm}=0.122\ \mathrm m\)
Step 2: \(c=2.45\times10^9\times0.122\)
Step 3: \(c=2.99\times10^8\ \mathrm{m/s}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{expected spacing }=\frac{c}{2f}=\frac{3.0\times10^8}{4.9\times10^9}=6.12\ \mathrm{cm}\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[\text{microwave range }1\ \mathrm{mm}\text{ to }0.3\ \mathrm m:\ 12.2\ \mathrm{cm}\text{ lies inside}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the oven is a metal box, so waves reflect and superpose; energy is deposited where the electric field oscillates most strongly, at the antinodes}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{antinodes are half a wavelength apart}\); (C) \(\text{a quarter wavelength separates a node from an antinode}\); (D) \(\text{microwaves are electromagnetic}\).
Key point: \(\text{antinode spacing}=\lambda/2;\ c=f\lambda\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Deviation of red and violet light by a thin prism, its angular dispersion and why violet is deviated more
questions.question: A thin glass prism of angle 6.0° has refractive index 1.514 for red and 1.532 for violet light. What is the angular dispersion, and which statement is correct?
options: A) 0.018°; red is deviated more because its wavelength is longer
B) 3.14° for both colours, because a thin prism does not disperse light

C) The violet deviation is \(0.532\times6.0^\circ=3.19^\circ\) and the red is \(0.514\times6.0^\circ=3.08^\circ\), so the angular dispersion is 0.108°; violet is deviated more because glass has a larger refractive index for shorter wavelengths, i.e. light travels slower in glass at higher frequencies
D) 0.108°; the deviation of a thin prism is \(nA\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\delta_v=3.19^\circ,\ \delta_r=3.08^\circ\); dispersion \(0.108^\circ\).
Given: \(A=6.0^\circ,\ n_r=1.514,\ n_v=1.532\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{thin prism: }\delta=(n-1)A;\ \text{angular dispersion}=\delta_v-\delta_r=(n_v-n_r)A\)
Step 1: \(\delta_v=(1.532-1)\times6.0^\circ=3.192^\circ\)
Step 2: \(\delta_r=(1.514-1)\times6.0^\circ=3.084^\circ\)
Step 3: \(\delta_v-\delta_r=0.108^\circ\)
Worked derivation: \[(n_v-n_r)A=0.018\times6.0^\circ=0.108^\circ\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[\text{mean }n=1.523\Rightarrow\delta\approx3.14^\circ,\ \text{between the two}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the refractive index of glass depends on wavelength (dispersion); a larger }n\text{ bends light more at each face}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{forgets to multiply by }A\text{; violet is deviated more}\); (B) \(\text{a thin prism still disperses}\); (D) \(\delta=(n-1)A\).
Key point: \(\delta=(n-1)A;\ \text{dispersion}=(n_v-n_r)A\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Refraction of water waves in a ripple tank at a boundary between deep and shallow water, finding speeds and the angle of refraction while the frequency stays fixed
questions.question: In a ripple tank driven at 10 Hz, the wavelength is 2.0 cm in deep water and 1.5 cm over a submerged glass plate (shallow water). Straight wavefronts meet the boundary at 30° incidence. Which result is correct?
options: A) The frequency drops to 7.5 Hz over the plate; the wave bends away from the normal
B) Speeds 20 cm/s and 15 cm/s; angle of refraction 42°
C) Speeds 0.2 cm/s and 0.15 cm/s; angle 30°, since the frequency is unchanged

D) Speeds are 20 cm/s (deep) and 15 cm/s (shallow); the frequency stays 10 Hz, fixed by the source; \(\sin r=\sin30^\circ\times\dfrac{15}{20}=0.375\Rightarrow r\approx22^\circ\), so the waves bend towards the normal on entering the slower (shallow) region
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(20\) and \(15\) cm/s; \(f=10\) Hz; \(r\approx22^\circ\).
Given: \(f=10\ \mathrm{Hz},\ \lambda_1=2.0\ \mathrm{cm},\ \lambda_2=1.5\ \mathrm{cm},\ i=30^\circ\)
Formula/Principle: \(v=f\lambda;\ \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}=\dfrac{v_1}{v_2}\)
Step 1: \(v_1=10\times2.0=20\ \mathrm{cm/s};\ v_2=10\times1.5=15\ \mathrm{cm/s}\)
Step 2: \(\sin r=\sin30^\circ\times\dfrac{15}{20}=0.5\times0.75=0.375\)
Step 3: \(r=\sin^{-1}0.375\approx22.0^\circ\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{\sin30^\circ}{\sin22.0^\circ}=\frac{0.500}{0.375}=1.33=\frac{20}{15}\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[r<i\text{ because }v_2<v_1\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the frequency is set by the vibrator and cannot change at a boundary, so a change in speed shows up as a change in wavelength and direction (Huygens' construction)}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{frequency is unchanged; it bends towards the normal}\); (B) \(\text{uses }\sin r=\sin i\times v_1/v_2\text{, wrong}\); (C) \(\text{wrong units and no bending}\).
Key point: \(\text{refraction: }f\text{ fixed},\ \frac{\sin i}{\sin r}=\frac{v_1}{v_2}=\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Counting the spectral lines emitted as hydrogen atoms excited to n = 4 return to the ground state, and finding the longest and shortest wavelengths and the visible lines
questions.question: A sample of hydrogen atoms is excited to the \(n=4\) level. Which statement about the emitted lines is correct (\(R=1.097\times10^7\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}\))?
options: A) 6 lines can appear; the longest wavelength is 1875 nm (\(4\to3\), infrared), the shortest is 97.2 nm (\(4\to1\), ultraviolet), and two lines, 486 nm (\(4\to2\)) and 656 nm (\(3\to2\)), are visible
B) 3 lines appear; the shortest is \(4\to3\)
C) 6 lines appear; the longest is \(4\to1\), because it has the largest energy
D) 4 lines appear, all in the visible region
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(6\) lines; longest \(1875\) nm; shortest \(97.2\) nm; visible \(486\) and \(656\) nm.
Given: \(n_{\text{initial}}=4,\ R=1.097\times10^7\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{lines}=\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2};\ \dfrac1\lambda=R\left(\dfrac1{n_f^2}-\dfrac1{n_i^2}\right)\)
Step 1: \(\text{lines}=\dfrac{4\times3}{2}=6:\ 4\to3,4\to2,4\to1,3\to2,3\to1,2\to1\)
Step 2: \(4\to3:\ \dfrac1\lambda=R\cdot\dfrac{7}{144}=5.333\times10^5\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}\Rightarrow\lambda=1875\ \mathrm{nm}\)
Step 3: \(4\to1:\ \dfrac1\lambda=R\cdot\dfrac{15}{16}=1.0284\times10^7\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}\Rightarrow\lambda=97.2\ \mathrm{nm}\)
Worked derivation: \[4\to2:\ R\cdot\tfrac{3}{16}\Rightarrow486\ \mathrm{nm};\quad3\to2:\ R\cdot\tfrac{5}{36}\Rightarrow656\ \mathrm{nm}\]
Check: \[\text{visible range }400\text{–}700\ \mathrm{nm}\text{ contains only the two Balmer lines}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the smallest energy gap (between the closest high levels) gives the longest wavelength; the largest gap (to the ground state) gives the shortest}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{a sample has atoms taking every route}\); (C) \(\text{largest energy means shortest wavelength}\); (D) \(\text{only two lines are visible}\).
Key point: \(\text{lines}=\frac{n(n-1)}{2};\ \lambda\propto\frac{1}{\Delta E}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Energy released by the complete fission of 1 kg of uranium-235 at 200 MeV per fission, in joules and kilowatt-hours
questions.question: Each fission of U-235 releases about 200 MeV. If all the nuclei in 1.0 kg of U-235 undergo fission, about how much energy is released (\(N_A=6.02\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}\), \(1\ \mathrm{MeV}=1.6\times10^{-13}\) J)?
options: A) \(8.2\times10^{13}\) J, about \(2.3\times10^7\) kWh
C) \(8.2\times10^{10}\) J, about \(2.3\times10^4\) kWh
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\approx8.2\times10^{13}\) J \(\approx2.3\times10^7\) kWh.
Given: \(m=1000\ \mathrm g,\ M=235\ \mathrm{g/mol},\ E_{\text{fission}}=200\ \mathrm{MeV}\)
Formula/Principle: \(N=\dfrac{m}{M}N_A;\ E=N\times E_{\text{fission}};\ 1\ \mathrm{kWh}=3.6\times10^6\ \mathrm J\)
Step 1: \(N=\dfrac{1000}{235}\times6.02\times10^{23}=2.56\times10^{24}\)
Step 2: \(E=2.56\times10^{24}\times200=5.12\times10^{26}\ \mathrm{MeV}=5.12\times10^{26}\times1.6\times10^{-13}=8.2\times10^{13}\ \mathrm J\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{8.2\times10^{13}}{3.6\times10^6}=2.3\times10^7\ \mathrm{kWh}\)
Worked derivation: \[\Delta m=\frac{E}{c^2}=\frac{8.2\times10^{13}}{9\times10^{16}}\approx0.9\ \mathrm g\ \text{of the 1 kg}\]
Check: \[\text{burning 1 kg of coal gives }\sim3\times10^7\ \mathrm J;\ \text{fission is}\sim10^{6}\text{ times more}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{fission releases about 0.9 MeV per nucleon, a million times the few eV per atom of chemical reactions}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{forgets to convert MeV to J}\); (C) \(\text{uses 1 g}\); (D) \(\text{energy of one fission in MeV}\).
Key point: \(N=\frac{m}{M}N_A;\ 200\ \mathrm{MeV}\text{ per fission}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Using dimensional analysis to find how the speed of deep-water gravity waves and of capillary ripples depends on wavelength, and which waves travel faster
questions.question: The speed of long waves on deep water depends only on \(g\) and wavelength \(\lambda\); that of short ripples only on surface tension \(\sigma\), density \(\rho\) and \(\lambda\). Which conclusion follows from dimensional analysis?
options: A) Both speeds are independent of \(\lambda\)
B) Gravity waves: \(v\propto\sqrt{g/\lambda}\); ripples: \(v\propto\sqrt{\sigma\lambda/\rho}\)
C) Gravity waves: \(v\propto g\lambda\); ripples: \(v\propto\sigma/(\rho\lambda)\)

D) Gravity waves: \(v\propto\sqrt{g\lambda}\), so longer waves travel faster; ripples: \(v\propto\sqrt{\dfrac{\sigma}{\rho\lambda}}\), so shorter ripples travel faster; doubling \(\lambda\) multiplies the gravity-wave speed by \(\sqrt2\) and divides the ripple speed by \(\sqrt2\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(v\propto\sqrt{g\lambda}\); \(v\propto\sqrt{\sigma/(\rho\lambda)}\).
Given: \([g]=\mathrm{LT^{-2}},\ [\lambda]=\mathrm L,\ [\sigma]=\mathrm{MT^{-2}},\ [\rho]=\mathrm{ML^{-3}}\)
Formula/Principle: \(v=kg^a\lambda^b;\ v=k\sigma^x\rho^y\lambda^z;\ \text{match powers of M, L, T}\)
Step 1: \(\mathrm{LT^{-1}}=\mathrm{L^{a+b}T^{-2a}}\Rightarrow a=\tfrac12,\ b=\tfrac12\Rightarrow v\propto\sqrt{g\lambda}\)
Step 2: \(\mathrm{LT^{-1}}=\mathrm{M^{x+y}L^{-3y+z}T^{-2x}}\Rightarrow x=\tfrac12,\ y=-\tfrac12,\ z=-\tfrac12\)
Step 3: \(v\propto\sqrt{\dfrac{\sigma}{\rho\lambda}}\)
Worked derivation: \[\lambda\to2\lambda:\ \sqrt{g\lambda}\to\sqrt2\sqrt{g\lambda};\quad\sqrt{\tfrac{\sigma}{\rho\lambda}}\to\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\sqrt{\tfrac{\sigma}{\rho\lambda}}\]
Check: \[\text{M: }x+y=0;\ \text{L: }-3y+z=\tfrac32-\tfrac12=1;\ \text{T: }-2x=-1\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{only one combination of the given quantities has dimensions of speed, fixing the dependence on }\lambda\text{ up to a constant}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{both depend on }\lambda\); (B) \(\text{dimensions are not speed}\); (C) \(\text{not speed dimensions}\).
Key point: \(\text{deep water }v\propto\sqrt{g\lambda};\ \text{ripples }v\propto\sqrt{\sigma/\rho\lambda}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Recoil of a rifle from conservation of momentum, the impulse on the bullet and the average force over the time in the barrel
questions.question: A 3.0 kg rifle fires a 30 g bullet at 500 m/s; the bullet spends 5.0 ms in the barrel. Which result is correct?
options: A) Recoil speed 50 m/s; impulse 1.5 N s
B) Recoil speed 500 m/s, because momentum is shared equally
C) Recoil speed 5.0 m/s; impulse on the bullet 15 N s; average force 3000 N; the rifle receives an equal and opposite impulse, so the total momentum stays zero
D) Recoil speed 5.0 m/s; average force 75 N
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(5.0\) m/s; \(15\) N s; \(3000\) N.
Given: \(M=3.0\ \mathrm{kg},\ m=0.030\ \mathrm{kg},\ v=500\ \mathrm{m/s},\ \Delta t=5.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm s\)
Formula/Principle: \(0=mv+MV;\ J=\Delta p;\ F_{\text{avg}}=\dfrac{J}{\Delta t}\)
Step 1: \(V=-\dfrac{mv}{M}=-\dfrac{0.030\times500}{3.0}=-5.0\ \mathrm{m/s}\)
Step 2: \(J=mv=0.030\times500=15\ \mathrm{N\,s}\)
Step 3: \(F=\dfrac{15}{5.0\times10^{-3}}=3000\ \mathrm N\)
Worked derivation: \[MV=3.0\times(-5.0)=-15\ \mathrm{N\,s}=-J\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[\text{KE: bullet }3750\ \mathrm J,\ \text{rifle }37.5\ \mathrm J\ (\text{ratio }M/m=100)\]
Why: \(\text{no external horizontal force acts during firing, so the momentum gained by the bullet is matched by the rifle's backward momentum}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{factor 10 errors}\); (B) \(\text{momentum, not speed, is equal and opposite}\); (D) \(\text{force miscalculated}\).
Key point: \(MV=-mv;\ F_{\text{avg}}=\Delta p/\Delta t\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Fraction of kinetic energy transferred in a one-dimensional elastic collision with a stationary target, and why light nuclei make good neutron moderators
questions.question: A neutron (mass 1 u) collides head-on elastically with a stationary carbon-12 nucleus. What fraction of its kinetic energy does it lose, and which statement is correct?
options: A) All its kinetic energy, because the collision is elastic

B) \(\dfrac{48}{169}\approx0.28\); the neutron rebounds with \(\dfrac{11}{13}\) of its speed, keeping \(\dfrac{121}{169}\approx0.72\) of its kinetic energy; the fraction transferred is \(\dfrac{4m_1m_2}{(m_1+m_2)^2}\), which would be 1 for equal masses, so light nuclei slow neutrons best
C) \(\dfrac{1}{12}\), the mass ratio
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\frac{48}{169}\approx0.28\) of its kinetic energy.
Given: \(m_1=1\ \mathrm u,\ m_2=12\ \mathrm u,\ u_2=0,\ \text{elastic, head-on}\)
Formula/Principle: \(v_1=\dfrac{m_1-m_2}{m_1+m_2}u_1,\ v_2=\dfrac{2m_1}{m_1+m_2}u_1\)
Step 1: \(v_1=\dfrac{1-12}{13}u_1=-\dfrac{11}{13}u_1\)
Step 2: \(\text{KE retained}=\left(\dfrac{11}{13}\right)^2=\dfrac{121}{169}\)
Step 3: \(\text{KE transferred}=1-\dfrac{121}{169}=\dfrac{48}{169}\approx0.284\)
