Worked derivation: \[\frac{4m_1m_2}{(m_1+m_2)^2}=\frac{4\times12}{169}=\frac{48}{169}\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[\text{momentum: }u_1=-\tfrac{11}{13}u_1+12\times\tfrac{2}{13}u_1=\tfrac{13}{13}u_1\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{energy transfer is greatest when the masses are equal; a heavy target merely reflects the light projectile}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{only equal masses give full transfer}\); (C) \(\text{not the energy ratio}\); (D) \(\text{that is the speed ratio of the rebound}\).
Key point: \(\text{elastic transfer fraction}=\frac{4m_1m_2}{(m_1+m_2)^2}\)

questions.sub_topic: Finding the mass of a uniform metre rule from the balance point when a known mass hangs from it, using the principle of moments
questions.question: A uniform metre rule balances on a knife-edge at the 40 cm mark when a 100 g mass hangs at the 10 cm mark. What is the mass of the rule, and which condition is used?
options: A) 75 g; only the net force must be zero

B) 300 g; for equilibrium of a rigid body both the net force and the net torque about any point must be zero; about the knife-edge, \(100\times(40-10)=M\times(50-40)\), and the knife-edge pushes up with a force equal to the weight of 400 g
C) 33 g; the weight of the rule acts at the knife-edge
D) 100 g, because the system balances
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(M=300\) g; knife-edge reaction \(=0.40\ \mathrm{kg}\times g\).
Given: \(\text{pivot }40\ \mathrm{cm};\ 100\ \mathrm g\text{ at }10\ \mathrm{cm};\ \text{rule's centre of gravity at }50\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\sum\tau=0;\ \sum F=0\)
Step 1: \(\text{anticlockwise moment}=100g\times30\)
Step 2: \(\text{clockwise moment}=Mg\times10\)
Step 3: \(3000=10M\Rightarrow M=300\ \mathrm g;\ N=(100+300)g\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{moments about the 0 cm end: }N(40)=100(10)+300(50)=16000\Rightarrow N=400\ \mathrm{g\text{-wt}}\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[\text{a heavier rule needs the pivot closer to its centre; }300\text{ g with lever arm 10 cm balances }100\text{ g at 30 cm}\]
Why: \(\text{the weight of a uniform rule acts at its midpoint, so it supplies a moment about any pivot not at the centre}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{torque balance is essential}\); (C) \(\text{the centre of gravity is at 50 cm}\); (D) \(\text{lever arms differ}\).
Key point: \(\text{equilibrium: }\sum F=0\text{ and }\sum\tau=0\)

questions.sub_topic: Applying Kepler's third law to compare the orbital period of a low-orbit space station with that of a geostationary satellite, and their orbital speeds
questions.question: A space station orbits at radius 6770 km with period 92.6 min. Using Kepler's third law, what is the period at orbital radius 42 200 km, and the orbital speeds?
options: A) about 24 h (1440 min), the geostationary orbit; speeds 7.66 km/s (station) and 3.07 km/s
B) about 9.6 h; speeds equal, since gravity is the same
C) about 577 min; speed 7.66 km/s at both radii
D) about 24 h; the higher satellite is faster
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\approx24\) h; \(7.66\) and \(3.07\) km/s.
Given: \(r_1=6770\ \mathrm{km},\ T_1=92.6\ \mathrm{min},\ r_2=42\,200\ \mathrm{km}\)
Formula/Principle: \(T^2\propto r^3\Rightarrow T_2=T_1\left(\dfrac{r_2}{r_1}\right)^{3/2};\ v=\dfrac{2\pi r}{T}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{r_2}{r_1}=\dfrac{42\,200}{6770}=6.233\)
Step 2: \(6.233^{3/2}=6.233\times2.497=15.56\Rightarrow T_2=92.6\times15.56=1441\ \mathrm{min}\approx24.0\ \mathrm h\)
Step 3: \(v_1=\dfrac{2\pi\times6.77\times10^6}{5556}=7.66\ \mathrm{km/s};\ v_2=\dfrac{2\pi\times4.22\times10^7}{86\,400}=3.07\ \mathrm{km/s}\)
Worked derivation: \[v\propto r^{-1/2}:\ \frac{v_2}{v_1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6.233}}=0.40;\ 7.66\times0.40=3.07\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[\text{a period of one sidereal day keeps the satellite above one point on the equator}\]
Why: \(\text{gravity provides the centripetal force: }\frac{GMm}{r^2}=\frac{m4\pi^2r}{T^2}\Rightarrow T^2=\frac{4\pi^2}{GM}r^3\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{uses }T\propto r\); (C) \(\text{uses }T\propto r\text{ and wrong speeds}\); (D) \(\text{higher orbits are slower}\).
Key point: \(T^2\propto r^3;\ v\propto r^{-1/2}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Work needed to split a liquid drop into many identical droplets, from surface energy and the increase in total surface area
questions.question: A water drop of radius 1.0 mm is sprayed into 1000 identical droplets. What work is needed (surface tension 0.072 N/m), and why?
options: A) Zero, because volume is conserved
B) \(9.0\times10^{-7}\) J, because the area increases by a factor 1000

D) \(8.1\times10^{-6}\) J: each droplet has radius 0.10 mm (volume conserved, \(r=R/10\)), the total surface area grows tenfold from \(4\pi R^2\) to \(1000\times4\pi r^2\), and the work equals surface tension times the increase in area
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(W\approx8.1\times10^{-6}\) J.
Given: \(R=1.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm m,\ n=1000,\ \sigma=0.072\ \mathrm{N/m}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\tfrac43\pi R^3=n\cdot\tfrac43\pi r^3;\ W=\sigma\,\Delta A\)
Step 1: \(r=\dfrac{R}{n^{1/3}}=\dfrac{1.0}{10}\ \mathrm{mm}=1.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm m\)
Step 2: \(\Delta A=4\pi(nr^2-R^2)=4\pi(1000\times10^{-8}-10^{-6})=4\pi\times9\times10^{-6}=1.131\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2}\)
Step 3: \(W=0.072\times1.131\times10^{-4}=8.14\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm J\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{A_{\text{final}}}{A_{\text{initial}}}=\frac{nr^2}{R^2}=\frac{1000}{100}=10\]
Check: \[\text{units: }\mathrm{N/m}\times\mathrm{m^2}=\mathrm{N\,m}=\mathrm J\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{surface energy per unit area equals surface tension; making new surface means pulling molecules from the interior to the surface against cohesion}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{area increases}\); (B) \(\text{area grows by 10, not 1000}\); (C) \(\text{factor 10 error}\).
Key point: \(\text{splitting into }n\text{ drops: area}\times n^{1/3};\ W=\sigma\Delta A\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Newton's law of cooling in its average form over successive intervals, the T⁴ dependence of radiated power, and good absorbers being good emitters
questions.question: Water cools from 90 °C to 70 °C in 5 min in a room at 30 °C. Using Newton's law of cooling (average-temperature form), which statement is correct?
options: A) In the next 5 min it cools to 50 °C, since cooling is uniform; a black body radiates less than a polished body at the same temperature
B) It cools to 60 °C in the next 5 min; doubling the absolute temperature doubles radiated power

C) In the next 5 min it cools to about 56.7 °C, because the rate of cooling is proportional to the excess temperature, which is now smaller; by Stefan's law, doubling the absolute temperature of a body multiplies its radiated power by 16; a good absorber is also a good emitter, so a dull black body radiates more than a shiny one at the same temperature
D) It reaches 30 °C in 10 min
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\approx56.7\ ^\circ\mathrm C\); \(P\propto T^4\Rightarrow\times16\); good absorbers emit well.
Given: \(90\to70\ ^\circ\mathrm C\text{ in }5\ \mathrm{min};\ T_0=30\ ^\circ\mathrm C\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac{T_1-T_2}{t}=k\left(\dfrac{T_1+T_2}{2}-T_0\right);\ P=\sigma AT^4\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{20}{5}=k(80-30)\Rightarrow k=0.08\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{70-T}{5}=0.08\left(\dfrac{70+T}{2}-30\right)\Rightarrow70-T=2+0.2T\)
Step 3: \(1.2T=68\Rightarrow T=56.7\ ^\circ\mathrm C\)
Worked derivation: \[P\propto T^4:\ (2T)^4=16T^4\]
Check: \[\text{drop in 2nd interval }13.3\ ^\circ\mathrm C<20\ ^\circ\mathrm C\text{ in the 1st}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{heat loss rate depends on the temperature excess over surroundings; as the body cools the excess shrinks, so cooling slows}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{cooling is not uniform; black bodies radiate most}\); (B) \(\text{wrong temperature and power law}\); (D) \(\text{approach to room temperature is gradual}\).
Key point: \(\text{rate of cooling}\propto(T-T_0);\ P\propto T^4\)

questions.sub_topic: Net work, change in internal energy and net heat for an ideal gas taken round a rectangular cycle on a P–V diagram in the clockwise sense
questions.question: An ideal gas is taken clockwise round a rectangular cycle on a P–V diagram between pressures \(1.0\times10^5\) Pa and \(3.0\times10^5\) Pa and volumes 1.0 L and 4.0 L. Which statement is correct?
options: A) Net work done by the gas is zero, since it returns to its initial state
B) Net work done by the gas is 1200 J, and the internal energy increases by 1200 J

C) Net work done by the gas is +600 J (the enclosed area); \(\Delta U=0\) over the cycle because internal energy is a state function; so the net heat absorbed is 600 J; reversing the direction (anticlockwise) makes the net work done on the gas 600 J
D) Net work done by the gas is −600 J, because the cycle is clockwise
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(W_{\text{net}}=+600\) J; \(\Delta U=0\); \(Q_{\text{net}}=600\) J.
Given: \(\Delta P=2.0\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa},\ \Delta V=3.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^3},\ \text{clockwise}\)
Formula/Principle: \(W_{\text{net}}=\oint P\,dV=\text{enclosed area};\ \Delta U_{\text{cycle}}=0;\ Q=\Delta U+W\)
Step 1: \(\text{expansion at }3.0\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}:\ W_1=3.0\times10^5\times3.0\times10^{-3}=900\ \mathrm J\)
Step 2: \(\text{compression at }1.0\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}:\ W_2=-1.0\times10^5\times3.0\times10^{-3}=-300\ \mathrm J;\ \text{isochoric steps: }0\)
Step 3: \(W_{\text{net}}=600\ \mathrm J;\ Q_{\text{net}}=0+600=600\ \mathrm J\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{area}=(3.0-1.0)\times10^5\times(4.0-1.0)\times10^{-3}=600\ \mathrm J\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[\text{clockwise}\Rightarrow\text{expansion happens at the higher pressure}\Rightarrow W_{\text{net}}>0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{more work is done by the gas when expanding at high pressure than is done on it when compressed at low pressure}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{work is not a state function}\); (B) \(\Delta U=0\text{ over a cycle and the area is 600 J}\); (D) \(\text{clockwise gives positive work by the gas}\).
Key point: \(\text{cycle: }\Delta U=0,\ Q=W=\text{enclosed area (clockwise positive)}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Root-mean-square speed of nitrogen molecules at room temperature from kinetic theory, the pressure relation and the average kinetic energy per molecule
questions.question: For nitrogen (\(M=0.028\ \mathrm{kg/mol}\)) at 300 K, which result is correct (\(R=8.314\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}\), \(k_B=1.38\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{J/K}\))?
options: A) \(v_{\text{rms}}=16.4\ \mathrm{m/s}\); average KE depends on molar mass

B) \(v_{\text{rms}}=\sqrt{3RT/M}\approx517\ \mathrm{m/s}\); kinetic theory gives \(P=\tfrac13\rho v_{\text{rms}}^2\); the average translational KE per molecule is \(\tfrac32k_BT=6.2\times10^{-21}\) J, the same for every gas at 300 K, so lighter molecules move faster
C) \(v_{\text{rms}}=298\ \mathrm{m/s}\); KE per molecule \(4.1\times10^{-21}\) J
D) \(v_{\text{rms}}=517\ \mathrm{m/s}\); \(P=\rho v_{\text{rms}}^2\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(v_{\text{rms}}\approx517\) m/s; \(\bar{KE}=6.2\times10^{-21}\) J.
Given: \(M=0.028\ \mathrm{kg/mol},\ T=300\ \mathrm K\)
Formula/Principle: \(v_{\text{rms}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}};\ P=\tfrac13\rho\overline{v^2};\ \overline{KE}=\tfrac32k_BT\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{3RT}{M}=\dfrac{3\times8.314\times300}{0.028}=2.672\times10^5\ \mathrm{m^2/s^2}\)
Step 2: \(v_{\text{rms}}=\sqrt{2.672\times10^5}=517\ \mathrm{m/s}\)
Step 3: \(\overline{KE}=1.5\times1.38\times10^{-23}\times300=6.21\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm J\)
Worked derivation: \[\tfrac12m v_{\text{rms}}^2=\tfrac12\cdot\frac{0.028}{6.02\times10^{23}}\cdot2.672\times10^5=6.21\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm J\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[\text{H}_2\ (M=0.002):\ v_{\text{rms}}=517\sqrt{14}\approx1930\ \mathrm{m/s}\]
Why: \(\text{temperature measures average translational KE per molecule; at fixed KE, speed varies as }1/\sqrt{m}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{uses }M=28\text{ instead of }0.028\ \mathrm{kg/mol}\text{; KE is independent of }M\); (C) \(\text{uses }\sqrt{RT/M}\text{ and }k_BT\text{, dropping the factors 3 and }\tfrac32\); (D) \(\text{factor }1/3\text{ missing}\).
Key point: \(v_{\text{rms}}=\sqrt{3RT/M};\ \overline{KE}=\frac32k_BT\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: How the period of a mass–spring oscillator changes when the spring is cut in half, springs are combined in series or parallel, or the mass is increased
questions.question: A 1.0 kg mass on a spring of force constant 100 N/m has period \(T_0\). Which set of results is correct?
options: A) \(T_0=0.10\) s; half the spring gives \(2T_0\)
B) \(T_0=0.63\) s; adding mass does not change the period
C) \(T_0=0.63\) s; two springs in parallel give \(\sqrt2\,T_0\)

D) \(T_0=2\pi\sqrt{m/k}=0.63\) s; cutting the spring in half doubles \(k\), giving \(T_0/\sqrt2=0.44\) s; two identical springs in series have \(k/2\) (period \(\sqrt2\,T_0=0.89\) s) and in parallel \(2k\) (period \(T_0/\sqrt2\)); making the mass 4.0 kg doubles the period to 1.26 s
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(T_0=0.63\) s; half spring \(0.44\) s; series \(0.89\) s; parallel \(0.44\) s; \(4m\Rightarrow1.26\) s.
Given: \(m=1.0\ \mathrm{kg},\ k=100\ \mathrm{N/m}\)
Formula/Principle: \(T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac mk};\ k\propto\dfrac{1}{\text{length}};\ \text{series }\dfrac1{k_s}=\dfrac1{k_1}+\dfrac1{k_2};\ \text{parallel }k_p=k_1+k_2\)
Step 1: \(T_0=2\pi\sqrt{0.01}=0.628\ \mathrm s\)
Step 2: \(\text{half spring: }k=200\ \mathrm{N/m}\Rightarrow T=0.628/\sqrt2=0.444\ \mathrm s\)
Step 3: \(\text{series }k=50\Rightarrow T=0.889\ \mathrm s;\ \text{parallel }k=200\Rightarrow0.444\ \mathrm s;\ m=4\Rightarrow T=1.257\ \mathrm s\)
Worked derivation: \[T\propto\sqrt{m/k}:\ \frac{T_{4m}}{T_0}=\sqrt4=2\]
Check: \[\text{units: }\sqrt{\mathrm{kg}/(\mathrm{N/m})}=\sqrt{\mathrm{s^2}}=\mathrm s\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a shorter spring stretches less per newton (stiffer); a larger mass has more inertia, so it oscillates more slowly}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(T_0\text{ wrong; half spring shortens the period}\); (B) \(T\propto\sqrt m\); (C) \(\text{parallel shortens the period}\).
Key point: \(T=2\pi\sqrt{m/k};\ \text{half spring }2k;\ \text{series }k/2;\ \text{parallel }2k\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Superposition of two equal and opposite pulses on a string at the instant they overlap, where the energy is at that moment, and how standing waves differ from travelling waves
questions.question: Two identical-shaped pulses, one upright and one inverted, travel towards each other on a stretched string. Which statement is correct?
options: A) At the instant of complete overlap the string is momentarily straight, but the energy has not vanished: it is all kinetic, since the string elements are moving; the pulses then emerge unchanged and continue; in a standing wave formed by two equal waves travelling in opposite directions, nodes are \(\lambda/2\) apart and no net energy is carried along the string
B) The pulses cancel permanently and their energy is converted to heat
C) The pulses reflect off each other like colliding balls
D) In a standing wave, energy travels along the string at the wave speed
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Momentarily flat with all energy kinetic; pulses pass through unchanged; standing waves carry no net energy, nodes \(\lambda/2\) apart.
Given: \(y_1=f(x-vt),\ y_2=-f(x+vt)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{superposition: }y=y_1+y_2;\ \text{velocity of an element }\dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t}\)
Step 1: \(\text{at overlap }y=f(x)-f(x)=0\text{ everywhere: string flat, no stretching, so no potential energy}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t}=-vf'(x)-vf'(x)=-2vf'(x)\ne0\Rightarrow\text{elements are moving: energy is kinetic}\)
Step 3: \(\text{after overlap each pulse continues with its own shape (principle of superposition)}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{standing wave: }y=2A\sin kx\cos\omega t;\ \text{nodes at }kx=n\pi\Rightarrow x=\tfrac{n\lambda}{2}\]
Check: \[\text{energy before}=\text{energy at overlap}=\text{energy after (no dissipation)}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{displacements add, but so do velocities; equal and opposite pulses cancel displacement while doubling velocity, storing the energy as kinetic energy}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{the pulses re-emerge}\); (C) \(\text{waves pass through each other}\); (D) \(\text{energy in a standing wave is trapped between nodes}\).
Key point: \(\text{superposition: pulses pass through each other; momentary cancellation stores energy as KE}\)
